questions.question_html:
Let $\vec{a}=4\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k},\vec{b}=10\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and a vector $\vec{c}$ be such that $2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})+3(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=\vec{0}$ .

If $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=15$ , then $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: The unknown vector $\vec{c}$ is represented in 3D: $\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ Cross product of 2 vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ : $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \\ 10 & 2 & -1 \end{aligned}|=-5\hat{i}+34\hat{j}+18\hat{k}\dots..(i)$ Cross product of 2 vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ : $(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 10 & 2 & -1 \\ x & y & z \end{aligned}|=(2z+y)\hat{i}-(10z+x)\hat{j}+(10y-2x)\hat{k}\dots\dots(ii)$ We know, $2(a \times b)+3(b \times c)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2(-5\hat{i}+34\hat{j}+18\hat{k})+3{(2z+y)\hat{i}-(10z+x)\hat{j}+(10y-2x)\hat{k}}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(6z+3y-10)\hat{i}+(68-30z-3x)j+(36+30y-6x)\hat{k}=0$ As individual vector components of a null vector are zero. $\begin{aligned} x-5y & =6\dots.P_{1} \\ y+2z & =\frac{10}{3}\dots..P_{2} \\ 10z+x & =\frac{68}{3}\dots.P_{3} \end{aligned}$ $(\vec{a}) \cdot (\vec{c})=15 \Rightarrow (4\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \cdot (x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k})=4x-y+3z=15\dots\dots(iv)$ Equation set $(iii)$ is mathematically constructed to form a linear combination of 2 planes $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ generating the $3^{\text{rd}}$ plane $P_{3}$ : $x-5y+(𝝀) \cdot (y+2z)=\frac{68}{3} \Rightarrow 𝝀=5 \Rightarrow P_{1}+5P_{2}=P_{3}\dots\dots(v)$ Equation ( $v$ ) is conclusive in generating a family of planes ${P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}}$ indicating infinite solutions for the system equation (iii) We need an auxiliary equation provided through (iv) to render an unique solution for the vector $\vec{c}$ : $⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} x-5y & =6 & \dots. & P_{1} \\ y+2z & =\frac{10}{3} & \dots. & P_{2} \\ 4x-y+3z & =15 & \dots. & P_{4} \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥\dots.(vi)$ Equation (vi) can be solved using Determinants and Cramer's rule : $𝚫=|\begin{aligned} 1 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \end{aligned}| \le ftarrow R_{3}=R_{3}-4R_{1}=|\begin{aligned} 1 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 19 & 3 \end{aligned}|=-35\dots..(vii)$ $\Delta_{x}=|\begin{aligned} 6 & -5 & 0 \\ \frac{10}{3} & 1 & 2 \\ 15 & -1 & 3 \end{aligned}|$ $\begin{aligned} & R_{1}=R_{1}+5R_{2} \\ & R_{3}=R_{3}+R_{2} \end{aligned}$ $=|\begin{aligned} \frac{68}{3} & 0 & 10 \\ \frac{10}{3} & 1 & 2 \\ \frac{55}{3} & 0 & 5 \end{aligned}|$ $C_{1}⇆C_{2}$ $=-|\begin{aligned} 0 & \frac{68}{3} \\ 1 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 0 & \frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{55}{3} \end{aligned}|=(\frac{68}{3}) \cdot (5)-(\frac{55}{3}) \cdot (10)=-70\dots\dots(viii)$ Equations $(vii),(viii),(ix)$ and $(x)$ provides the solution to system equation $(vi)$ from Cramer's rule : $⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} x=\frac{\Delta_{x}}{\Delta}=\frac{70}{35}= \\ y=\frac{\Delta_{y}}{\Delta}=-\frac{28}{35}=-\frac{4}{5} \\ z=\frac{\Delta_{z}}{\Delta}=\frac{217}{(3) \cdot (35)}=\frac{31}{15} \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$ $\Rightarrow \vec{c}=(2)\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{5})\hat{j}+(\frac{31}{15})\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore (\vec{c}) \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \\ & ={(2)\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{5})\hat{j}+(\frac{31}{15})\hat{k}} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \\ & =2-\frac{4}{5}-\frac{31}{5} \end{aligned}$ $=-\frac{4+31-10}{5}=-5$
questions.explanation_html:
The unknown vector $\vec{c}$ is represented in 3D: $\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

Cross product of 2 vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ :

$(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \\ 10 & 2 & -1 \end{aligned}|=-5\hat{i}+34\hat{j}+18\hat{k}\dots..(i)$

Cross product of 2 vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ :

$(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 10 & 2 & -1 \\ x & y & z \end{aligned}|=(2z+y)\hat{i}-(10z+x)\hat{j}+(10y-2x)\hat{k}\dots\dots(ii)$

We know, $2(a \times b)+3(b \times c)=0$

$\Rightarrow 2(-5\hat{i}+34\hat{j}+18\hat{k})+3{(2z+y)\hat{i}-(10z+x)\hat{j}+(10y-2x)\hat{k}}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(6z+3y-10)\hat{i}+(68-30z-3x)j+(36+30y-6x)\hat{k}=0$

As individual vector components of a null vector are zero.

$\begin{aligned} x-5y & =6\dots.P_{1} \\ y+2z & =\frac{10}{3}\dots..P_{2} \\ 10z+x & =\frac{68}{3}\dots.P_{3} \end{aligned}$

$(\vec{a}) \cdot (\vec{c})=15 \Rightarrow (4\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \cdot (x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k})=4x-y+3z=15\dots\dots(iv)$

Equation set $(iii)$ is mathematically constructed to form a linear combination of 2 planes $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ generating the $3^{\text{rd}}$ plane $P_{3}$ :

$x-5y+(𝝀) \cdot (y+2z)=\frac{68}{3} \Rightarrow 𝝀=5 \Rightarrow P_{1}+5P_{2}=P_{3}\dots\dots(v)$

Equation ( $v$ ) is conclusive in generating a family of planes ${P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}}$ indicating infinite solutions for the system equation (iii)

We need an auxiliary equation provided through (iv) to render an unique solution for the vector $\vec{c}$ :

$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} x-5y & =6 & \dots. & P_{1} \\ y+2z & =\frac{10}{3} & \dots. & P_{2} \\ 4x-y+3z & =15 & \dots. & P_{4} \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥\dots.(vi)$

Equation (vi) can be solved using Determinants and Cramer's rule :

$𝚫=|\begin{aligned} 1 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 & 3 \end{aligned}| \le ftarrow R_{3}=R_{3}-4R_{1}=|\begin{aligned} 1 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 19 & 3 \end{aligned}|=-35\dots..(vii)$

$\Delta_{x}=|\begin{aligned} 6 & -5 & 0 \\ \frac{10}{3} & 1 & 2 \\ 15 & -1 & 3 \end{aligned}|$

$\begin{aligned} & R_{1}=R_{1}+5R_{2} \\ & R_{3}=R_{3}+R_{2} \end{aligned}$

$=|\begin{aligned} \frac{68}{3} & 0 & 10 \\ \frac{10}{3} & 1 & 2 \\ \frac{55}{3} & 0 & 5 \end{aligned}|$

$C_{1}⇆C_{2}$

$=-|\begin{aligned} 0 & \frac{68}{3} \\ 1 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 0 & \frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{55}{3} \end{aligned}|=(\frac{68}{3}) \cdot (5)-(\frac{55}{3}) \cdot (10)=-70\dots\dots(viii)$

Equations $(vii),(viii),(ix)$ and $(x)$ provides the solution to system equation $(vi)$ from Cramer's rule :

$⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} x=\frac{\Delta_{x}}{\Delta}=\frac{70}{35}= \\ y=\frac{\Delta_{y}}{\Delta}=-\frac{28}{35}=-\frac{4}{5} \\ z=\frac{\Delta_{z}}{\Delta}=\frac{217}{(3) \cdot (35)}=\frac{31}{15} \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥$

$\Rightarrow \vec{c}=(2)\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{5})\hat{j}+(\frac{31}{15})\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore (\vec{c}) \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \\ & ={(2)\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{5})\hat{j}+(\frac{31}{15})\hat{k}} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \\ & =2-\frac{4}{5}-\frac{31}{5} \end{aligned}$

$=-\frac{4+31-10}{5}=-5$

questions.question_text: Let $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ be unit vectors inclined at an acute angle such that $|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . If $\vec{A}=\lambda\hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v})$ , then $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Let $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ be unit vectors inclined at an acute angle such that $|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . If $\vec{A}=\lambda\hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v})$ , then $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Since $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ are unit vectors, $|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=|\hat{u}||\hat{v}|sin\theta=sin\theta$ Given $|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ So, $sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ The angle is acute, hence $\theta=60^{\circ} \Rightarrow \hat{u} \cdot \hat{v}=cos60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ Now, $\vec{A}=\lambda\hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v})$ We take dot product with $\hat{u}$ : $\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}=\lambda(\hat{u} \cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{v} \cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{u}$ Now, $\hat{u} \cdot \hat{u}=1,\hat{v} \cdot \hat{u}=\frac{1}{2},(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{u}=0$ Therefore, $\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}$ So, $\lambda=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}-\frac{1}{2}\text{(1)}$ Now take dot product with $\hat{v}$ : $\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}=\lambda(\hat{u} \cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{v} \cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{v}$ Using $\hat{u} \cdot \hat{v}=\frac{1}{2},\hat{v} \cdot \hat{v}=1,(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{v}=0$ we get $\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1$ Hence, $\frac{\lambda}{2}=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}-1 \Rightarrow \lambda=2(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v})-2\text{(2)}$ Now let $x=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u},y=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}$ Then from above, $x=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}\text{and}y=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1$ From the first, $\lambda=x-\frac{1}{2}$ Also, $x-2y=(\lambda+\frac{1}{2})-2(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1)=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}-\lambda-2=-\frac{3}{2}$ So we form $\lambda$ as a linear combination of $x$ and $y$ . Check Option A: $\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}y=\frac{4}{3}(\lambda+\frac{1}{2})-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1)$ $=\frac{4\lambda}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=\lambda$ Hence, $\lambda=\frac{4}{3}(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u})-\frac{2}{3}(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v})$ So the correct option is: $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
Since $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ are unit vectors,

$|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=|\hat{u}||\hat{v}|sin\theta=sin\theta$

Given

$|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

So,

$sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

The angle is acute, hence

$\theta=60^{\circ} \Rightarrow \hat{u} \cdot \hat{v}=cos60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$

Now,

$\vec{A}=\lambda\hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v})$

We take dot product with $\hat{u}$ :

$\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}=\lambda(\hat{u} \cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{v} \cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{u}$

Now,

$\hat{u} \cdot \hat{u}=1,\hat{v} \cdot \hat{u}=\frac{1}{2},(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{u}=0$

Therefore,

$\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}$

So,

$\lambda=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u}-\frac{1}{2}\text{(1)}$

Now take dot product with $\hat{v}$ :

$\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}=\lambda(\hat{u} \cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{v} \cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{v}$

Using

$\hat{u} \cdot \hat{v}=\frac{1}{2},\hat{v} \cdot \hat{v}=1,(\hat{u} \times \hat{v}) \cdot \hat{v}=0$

we get

$\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1$

Hence,

$\frac{\lambda}{2}=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}-1 \Rightarrow \lambda=2(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v})-2\text{(2)}$

Now let

$x=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u},y=\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v}$

Then from above,

$x=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}\text{and}y=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1$

From the first,

$\lambda=x-\frac{1}{2}$

Also,

$x-2y=(\lambda+\frac{1}{2})-2(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1)=\lambda+\frac{1}{2}-\lambda-2=-\frac{3}{2}$

So we form $\lambda$ as a linear combination of $x$ and $y$ .

Check Option A:

$\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}y=\frac{4}{3}(\lambda+\frac{1}{2})-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1)$

$=\frac{4\lambda}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=\lambda$

Hence,

$\lambda=\frac{4}{3}(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{u})-\frac{2}{3}(\vec{A} \cdot \hat{v})$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$

questions.question_text: Let P be a point in the plane of the vectors $\vec{AB}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{AC}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ such that P is equidistant from the lines AB and AC. If $|\vec{AP}|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ , then the area of the triangle ABP is :
questions.question_html: Let P be a point in the plane of the vectors $\vec{AB}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{AC}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ such that P is equidistant from the lines AB and AC. If $|\vec{AP}|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ , then the area of the triangle ABP is :
questions.explanation_text: Point $P$ is equidistant from the lines $AB$ and $AC$ . Geometrically, this means point $P$ must lie on the angle bisector of the angle formed by vectors $AB$ and $AC$ . First, we find the unit vectors along $AB$ and $AC$ : $|AB|=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$ $|AC|=\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$ Since the magnitudes are equal, the angle bisector $v$ is simply the sum of the two vectors: $\begin{aligned} v=AB+AC=(3+1)\hat{i}+(1-1)\hat{j}+(-1+3)\hat{k}=4\hat{i}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ The vector $AP$ will be in the direction of the unit vector $\hat{v}$ : $\hat{v}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{4^{2}+2^{2}}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{20}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{2\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}}$ Determine Vector $AP$ Given that $|AP|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ , we can write: $AP=|AP|\hat{v}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}(\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}})=\frac{1}{2}(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})=\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}$ Calculate the Area of Triangle $ABP$ The area of a triangle formed by two vectors $AB$ and $AP$ is given by the formula: $\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}|$ First, compute the cross product $AB \times AP$ : $\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}| \\ =\hat{i}(\frac{1}{2}-0)-\hat{j}(\frac{3}{2}-(-1))+\hat{k}(0-1) \\ =\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}-\frac{5}{2}\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ |\vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}|=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+(-\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{25}{4}+1}=\sqrt{\frac{26}{4}+\frac{4}{4}}=\sqrt{\frac{30}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2} \end{aligned}$ Finally, the area of the triangle is: Area $=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
Point $P$ is equidistant from the lines $AB$ and $AC$ . Geometrically, this means point $P$ must lie on the angle bisector of the angle formed by vectors $AB$ and $AC$ .

First, we find the unit vectors along $AB$ and $AC$ :

  • $|AB|=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$

  • $|AC|=\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$

Since the magnitudes are equal, the angle bisector $v$ is simply the sum of the two vectors:

$\begin{aligned} v=AB+AC=(3+1)\hat{i}+(1-1)\hat{j}+(-1+3)\hat{k}=4\hat{i}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

The vector $AP$ will be in the direction of the unit vector $\hat{v}$ :

$\hat{v}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{4^{2}+2^{2}}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{20}}=\frac{4\hat{i}+2\hat{k}}{2\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}}$

Determine Vector $AP$

Given that $|AP|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ , we can write:

$AP=|AP|\hat{v}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}(\frac{2\hat{i}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{5}})=\frac{1}{2}(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})=\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{k}$

  1. Calculate the Area of Triangle $ABP$

The area of a triangle formed by two vectors $AB$ and $AP$ is given by the formula:

$\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}|$

First, compute the cross product $AB \times AP$ :

$\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}| \\ =\hat{i}(\frac{1}{2}-0)-\hat{j}(\frac{3}{2}-(-1))+\hat{k}(0-1) \\ =\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}-\frac{5}{2}\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ |\vec{AB} \times \vec{AP}|=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+(-\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{25}{4}+1}=\sqrt{\frac{26}{4}+\frac{4}{4}}=\sqrt{\frac{30}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2} \end{aligned}$

Finally, the area of the triangle is:

Area $=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{4}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & (\vec{a}-\vec{b}) \cdot \vec{d}=\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{d} \\ & \because \vec{d}=\vec{c} \times \vec{a} \Rightarrow \vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=[\vec{a}\vec{c}\vec{a}]=0 \\ & \text{And}\vec{b} \cdot \vec{d}=\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{c} \times \vec{a}) \\ & =\vec{b} \cdot ((\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{a}) \\ & \Rightarrow (\vec{a}-\vec{b}) \cdot \vec{d}=\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})) \\ & =\vec{b} \cdot [\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}\vec{a}-\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}\vec{b}] \\ & =(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^{2}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}) \\ & =(-8)^{2}-6 \times 11=64-66=-2 \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Option (2) is correct.} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: If $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$ , then $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.question_html: If $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$ , then $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$ is equal to $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ We have to find $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$ given that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b}\text{and}\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$ Let $\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ Then $\vec{a}=(1,1,1),\vec{b}=(0,1,-1)$ Now compute $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}$ : $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x & y & z \end{aligned}|$ Expanding, $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\hat{i}(z-y)-\hat{j}(z-x)+\hat{k}(y-x)$ Since this is equal to $\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ , we compare components: $z-y=0$ $-(z-x)=1 \Rightarrow x-z=1$ $y-x=-1$ Also, from $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$ , $x+y+z=3$ Now solve the equations. From $z-y=0$ , $z=y$ From $x-z=1$ , $x=y+1$ Substitute into $x+y+z=3$ : $(y+1)+y+y=3$ $3y+1=3$ $3y=2 \Rightarrow y=\frac{2}{3}$ So, $z=\frac{2}{3},x=\frac{5}{3}$ Hence, $\vec{c}=\frac{5}{3}\hat{i}+\frac{2}{3}\hat{j}+\frac{2}{3}\hat{k}$ Now find $\vec{a}-2\vec{b}$ : $\vec{a}-2\vec{b}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-2(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$ $=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ Therefore, $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})=(\frac{5}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}) \cdot (1,-1,3)$ $=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+2$ $=\frac{3}{3}+2=1+2=3$ So, the required value is $3$
questions.explanation_html:
Let

$\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

We have to find

$\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$

given that

$\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b}\text{and}\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$

Let

$\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

Then

$\vec{a}=(1,1,1),\vec{b}=(0,1,-1)$

Now compute $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}$ :

$\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x & y & z \end{aligned}|$

Expanding,

$\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\hat{i}(z-y)-\hat{j}(z-x)+\hat{k}(y-x)$

Since this is equal to $\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ , we compare components:

$z-y=0$

$-(z-x)=1 \Rightarrow x-z=1$

$y-x=-1$

Also, from $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=3$ ,

$x+y+z=3$

Now solve the equations.

From $z-y=0$ ,

$z=y$

From $x-z=1$ ,

$x=y+1$

Substitute into $x+y+z=3$ :

$(y+1)+y+y=3$

$3y+1=3$

$3y=2 \Rightarrow y=\frac{2}{3}$

So,

$z=\frac{2}{3},x=\frac{5}{3}$

Hence,

$\vec{c}=\frac{5}{3}\hat{i}+\frac{2}{3}\hat{j}+\frac{2}{3}\hat{k}$

Now find $\vec{a}-2\vec{b}$ :

$\vec{a}-2\vec{b}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})-2(\hat{j}-\hat{k})$

$=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

Therefore,

$\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}-2\vec{b})=(\frac{5}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}) \cdot (1,-1,3)$

$=\frac{5}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+2$

$=\frac{3}{3}+2=1+2=3$

So, the required value is

$3$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . Then the square of the area of the triangle with adjacent sides determined by the vectors $(2\vec{a}+3\vec{b})$ and $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})$ is :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . Then the square of the area of the triangle with adjacent sides determined by the vectors $(2\vec{a}+3\vec{b})$ and $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k},\vec{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ We need the square of the area of the triangle whose adjacent sides are $2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}\text{and}\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ For two adjacent sides $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ , area of triangle is $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|$ So, square of the area is $(\frac{1}{2}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|^{2}$ Let $\vec{u}=2\vec{a}+3\vec{b},\vec{v}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ First find $\vec{u}$ : $2\vec{a}=2(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ $3\vec{b}=3(6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=18\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+9\hat{k}$ Therefore, $\vec{u}=2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}=22\hat{i}+15\hat{j}+15\hat{k}$ Now find $\vec{v}$ : $\vec{v}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}=(2-6)\hat{i}+(3-3)\hat{j}+(3-3)\hat{k}=-4\hat{i}$ Now compute $\vec{u} \times \vec{v}$ : $\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 22 & 15 & 15 \\ -4 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}|$ Expanding, $\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=\hat{i}(15 \cdot 0-15 \cdot 0)-\hat{j}(22 \cdot 0-15 \cdot (-4))+\hat{k}(22 \cdot 0-15 \cdot (-4))$ $=0\hat{i}-60\hat{j}+60\hat{k}$ So, $|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|^{2}=0^{2}+(-60)^{2}+60^{2}=3600+3600=7200$ Hence square of the area of the triangle is $\frac{1}{4} \times 7200=1800$ Therefore, the correct answer is $1800$ So, Option C is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Given

$\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k},\vec{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

We need the square of the area of the triangle whose adjacent sides are

$2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}\text{and}\vec{a}-\vec{b}$

For two adjacent sides $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ , area of triangle is

$\frac{1}{2}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|$

So, square of the area is

$(\frac{1}{2}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|^{2}$

Let

$\vec{u}=2\vec{a}+3\vec{b},\vec{v}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}$

First find $\vec{u}$ :

$2\vec{a}=2(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

$3\vec{b}=3(6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=18\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+9\hat{k}$

Therefore,

$\vec{u}=2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}=22\hat{i}+15\hat{j}+15\hat{k}$

Now find $\vec{v}$ :

$\vec{v}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}=(2-6)\hat{i}+(3-3)\hat{j}+(3-3)\hat{k}=-4\hat{i}$

Now compute $\vec{u} \times \vec{v}$ :

$\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 22 & 15 & 15 \\ -4 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}|$

Expanding,

$\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=\hat{i}(15 \cdot 0-15 \cdot 0)-\hat{j}(22 \cdot 0-15 \cdot (-4))+\hat{k}(22 \cdot 0-15 \cdot (-4))$

$=0\hat{i}-60\hat{j}+60\hat{k}$

So,

$|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|^{2}=0^{2}+(-60)^{2}+60^{2}=3600+3600=7200$

Hence square of the area of the triangle is

$\frac{1}{4} \times 7200=1800$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$1800$

So, Option C is correct.

If $\vec{c} \cdot (3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=10$ and $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=-2$ , then $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let the vectors $\vec{a}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ . For some $\lambda,\mu \in ℝ$ , let $\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\vec{b}$ .

If $\vec{c} \cdot (3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=10$ and $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=-2$ , then $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\vec{b}$ $\vec{c}=(\mu-\lambda)\hat{i}+(\lambda+3\mu)\hat{j}+(3\lambda+\mu)\hat{k}$ $\vec{c} \cdot (3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=10$ $3(\mu-\lambda)-6(\lambda+3\mu)+2(3\lambda+\mu)=10$ $-3\lambda-13\mu=10\dots(1)$ $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=-2$ $5\mu+3\lambda=-2\dots(2)$ Solving (1) & (2) $\lambda=1,\mu=-1$ $\vec{c}=-2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $|\vec{c}|^{2}=12$

$\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\vec{b}$

$\vec{c}=(\mu-\lambda)\hat{i}+(\lambda+3\mu)\hat{j}+(3\lambda+\mu)\hat{k}$

$\vec{c} \cdot (3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=10$

questions.question_text: For three unit vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ satisfying $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9\text{and}|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|=3\text{,}$ the positive value of k is :
questions.question_html:
For three unit vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ satisfying

$|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9\text{and}|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|=3\text{,}$

the positive value of k is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1$ $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}-2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}-2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{a}|^{2}-2\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $6+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})=9{|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1}$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=-\frac{3}{2}$ also, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=3+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})$ $=3+2(-\frac{3}{2})=3-3=0$ So $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=-\vec{c}$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{c}|^{2}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $1+1+2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=-\frac{1}{2}$ Similarly, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\frac{1}{2}\text{and}\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-\frac{1}{2}$ so, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=-\frac{1}{2}$ It is given that $|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|=3$ $\Rightarrow$ $|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|^{2}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $4|\vec{a}|^{2}+k^{2}|\vec{b}|^{2}+k^{2}|\vec{c}|^{2}+4k\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+2k^{2}\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+4k\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $4(1)^{2}+k^{2}(1)^{2}+k^{2}(1)^{2}+4k(-\frac{1}{2})+2k^{2}(-\frac{1}{2})+4k(-\frac{1}{2})=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $4+2k^{2}-2k-k^{2}-2k=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $k^{2}-4k-5=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(k-5)(k+1)=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $k=5,-1$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1$

$|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}-2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}-2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{a}|^{2}-2\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $6+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})=9{|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1}$

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=-\frac{3}{2}$

also,

$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=3+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})$

$=3+2(-\frac{3}{2})=3-3=0$

So

$\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=-\vec{c}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{c}|^{2}=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $1+1+2\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=-\frac{1}{2}$

Similarly,

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\frac{1}{2}\text{and}\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-\frac{1}{2}$

so,

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=-\frac{1}{2}$

It is given that

$|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|=3$

$\Rightarrow$ $|2\vec{a}+k\vec{b}+k\vec{c}|^{2}=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $4|\vec{a}|^{2}+k^{2}|\vec{b}|^{2}+k^{2}|\vec{c}|^{2}+4k\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+2k^{2}\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+4k\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $4(1)^{2}+k^{2}(1)^{2}+k^{2}(1)^{2}+4k(-\frac{1}{2})+2k^{2}(-\frac{1}{2})+4k(-\frac{1}{2})=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $4+2k^{2}-2k-k^{2}-2k=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $k^{2}-4k-5=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(k-5)(k+1)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $k=5,-1$

Let $\vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and $\vec{d}$ be a vector of magnitude 2 in $yz$ -plane. If $|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{53}$ , then the maximum possible value of $(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d})^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\lambda\hat{j}+2\hat{k},\lambda \in Z$ be two vectors. Let $\vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and $\vec{d}$ be a vector of magnitude 2 in $yz$ -plane. If $|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{53}$ , then the maximum possible value of $(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d})^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \bar{c}=\bar{a} \times \bar{b}=|\begin{aligned} \bar{i} & \bar{j} & \bar{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda & 2 \end{aligned}|=(2-\lambda)\bar{i}-\bar{j}(4)+(2\lambda)\bar{k} \\ & |\bar{c}|^{2}=53 \Rightarrow (2-\lambda)^{2}+16+(2\lambda)^{2}=53=5\lambda^{2}-4\lambda-33=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 5\lambda^{2}-15\lambda+11\lambda-33=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 5\lambda(\lambda-3)+11(\lambda-3)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow (\lambda-3)(5\lambda+11)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=3,\lambda \ne -\frac{11}{5}( \because \lambda \in Z) \\ & \therefore \bar{c}=(-1,-4,6) \end{aligned}$ Let $\therefore \bar{d}=(0,y,z)$ Given $|\bar{d}|=2 \Rightarrow y^{2}+z^{2}=4$ $\begin{aligned} & \bar{c}.\bar{d}=0-4y+6z \\ & (\bar{c}.\bar{d})^{2}=(-4y+6z)^{2} \\ & =16y^{2}+36z^{2}-48yz \\ & =16y^{2}+36(4-y^{2})-48y \cdot \sqrt{4-y^{2}} \end{aligned}$ Let $f(y)=-20y^{2}+144-48y\sqrt{4-y^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & f^{1}(y)=-40y-48(\sqrt{4-y^{2}})-48y(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4-y^{2}}})(-2y) \\ & =-40y-48(\frac{4-y^{2}-y^{2}}{\sqrt{4-y^{2}}}) \\ & f^{1}(y)=0⇐40y=96(\frac{y^{2}-2}{\sqrt{4-y^{2}}}) \\ & \Rightarrow 5y\sqrt{4-y^{2}}=12(y^{2}-2) \\ & \Rightarrow 25y^{2}(4-y^{2})=144(y^{4}+4-4y^{2}) \\ & =169y^{4}-676y^{2}+576=0 \\ & =169y^{4}-208y^{2}-468y^{2}+576=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 13y^{2}(13y^{2}-16)-36(13y^{2}-16)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow y^{2}=\frac{16}{13}(\text{or})\frac{36}{13} \\ & \Rightarrow y= \pm \frac{4}{\sqrt{13}}(\text{or}) \pm \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \\ & \therefore \text{Maximum of}(\bar{c}.\bar{d})^{2}=208 \end{aligned}$

Given $|\bar{d}|=2 \Rightarrow y^{2}+z^{2}=4$

questions.question_html: If the distance of the point $P(43,\alpha,\beta)$ , $\beta<0$ , from the line $\vec{r}=4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+3\hat{k}),\mu \in ℝ$ along a line with direction ratios $3,-1,0$ is $13\sqrt{10}$ , then $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is equal to ________
questions.explanation_text: Point $P$ : $(43,\alpha,\beta)$ with the constraint $\beta<0$ . Target Line ( $L_{1}$ ) : Given by $\vec{r}=4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+3\hat{k})$ . A general point $Q$ on this line is $(4+2\mu,0,-1+3\mu)$ . Direction of measurement : The distance is measured along a line with direction ratios $(3,-1,0)$ . Find Point $Q$ on the Target Line Since the distance is measured along the direction $d=(3,-1,0)$ , the vector $PQ$ must be parallel to $d$ . $\begin{aligned} PQ=Q-P=(4+2\mu-43,0-\alpha,-1+3\mu-\beta) \\ PQ=(2\mu-39,-\alpha,3\mu-\beta-1) \\ PQ=(2\mu-39,-\alpha,3\mu-\beta-1) \end{aligned}$ Because $PQ$ is parallel to $(3,-1,0)$ , their components must be proportional : 1. $\frac{2\mu-39}{3}=\frac{-\alpha}{-1}⟹2\mu-39=3\alpha⟹2\mu=3\alpha+39$ 2. $\frac{3\mu-\beta-1}{0}$ suggests the numerator must be zero for a finite ratio to exist: $3\mu-\beta-1=0⟹\beta=3\mu-1$ Calculate the Distance $PQ$ The distance $PQ$ is given as $13\sqrt{10}$ . Using the distance formula on the proportional components where the ratio is $k$ : $\begin{aligned} PQ=k(3,-1,0)=(3k,-k,0) \\ |PQ|=\sqrt{(3k)^{2}+(-k)^{2}+0^{2}}=\sqrt{10k^{2}}=|k|\sqrt{10} \end{aligned}$ Given $|PQ|=13\sqrt{10}$ , we find $|k|=13$ , so $k= \pm 13$ . Solve for $\alpha,\mu$ , and $\beta$ From our proportionality equations : $-\alpha=-k⟹\alpha=k$ $2\mu-39=3k$ Case 1 : $k=13$ $\alpha=13$ $2\mu-39=3(13)=39⟹2\mu=78⟹\mu=39$ $\beta=3\mu-1=3(39)-1=116$ Constraint Check : $\beta<0$ is False. (Reject this case) Case 2 : $k=-13$ $\alpha=-13$ $2\mu-39=3(-13)=-39⟹2\mu=0⟹\mu=0$ $\beta=3(0)-1=-1$ Constraint Check : $\beta<0$ is True. (Accept this case) $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(-13)^{2}+(-1)^{2}=169+1=170$ The value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is 170 .
questions.explanation_html:
• Point $P$ : $(43,\alpha,\beta)$ with the constraint $\beta<0$ .

  • Target Line ( $L_{1}$ ) : Given by $\vec{r}=4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+\mu(2\hat{i}+3\hat{k})$ .

    A general point $Q$ on this line is $(4+2\mu,0,-1+3\mu)$ .

  • Direction of measurement : The distance is measured along a line with direction ratios $(3,-1,0)$ .

Find Point $Q$ on the Target Line

Since the distance is measured along the direction $d=(3,-1,0)$ , the vector $PQ$ must be parallel to $d$ .

$\begin{aligned} PQ=Q-P=(4+2\mu-43,0-\alpha,-1+3\mu-\beta) \\ PQ=(2\mu-39,-\alpha,3\mu-\beta-1) \\ PQ=(2\mu-39,-\alpha,3\mu-\beta-1) \end{aligned}$

Because $PQ$ is parallel to $(3,-1,0)$ , their components must be proportional :

  1. 1. $\frac{2\mu-39}{3}=\frac{-\alpha}{-1}⟹2\mu-39=3\alpha⟹2\mu=3\alpha+39$
  1. 2. $\frac{3\mu-\beta-1}{0}$ suggests the numerator must be zero for a finite ratio to exist: $3\mu-\beta-1=0⟹\beta=3\mu-1$

Calculate the Distance $PQ$

The distance $PQ$ is given as $13\sqrt{10}$ . Using the distance formula on the proportional components where the ratio is $k$ :

$\begin{aligned} PQ=k(3,-1,0)=(3k,-k,0) \\ |PQ|=\sqrt{(3k)^{2}+(-k)^{2}+0^{2}}=\sqrt{10k^{2}}=|k|\sqrt{10} \end{aligned}$

Given $|PQ|=13\sqrt{10}$ , we find $|k|=13$ , so $k= \pm 13$ .

Solve for $\alpha,\mu$ , and $\beta$

From our proportionality equations :

  • $-\alpha=-k⟹\alpha=k$

  • $2\mu-39=3k$

Case 1 : $k=13$

  • $\alpha=13$

  • $2\mu-39=3(13)=39⟹2\mu=78⟹\mu=39$

  • $\beta=3\mu-1=3(39)-1=116$

  • Constraint Check : $\beta<0$ is False. (Reject this case)

Case 2 : $k=-13$

  • $\alpha=-13$

  • $2\mu-39=3(-13)=-39⟹2\mu=0⟹\mu=0$

  • $\beta=3(0)-1=-1$

  • Constraint Check : $\beta<0$ is True. (Accept this case)

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(-13)^{2}+(-1)^{2}=169+1=170$

The value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ is 170 .

If the side PS is rotated about the point P by an acute angle $\alpha$ in the plane of the parallelogram so that it becomes perpendicular to the side PQ, then $sin^{2}(\frac{5\alpha}{2})-sin^{2}(\frac{\alpha}{2})$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram PQRS are given by $\vec{PQ}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{PS}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ . If the side PS is rotated about the point P by an acute angle $\alpha$ in the plane of the parallelogram so that it becomes perpendicular to the side PQ, then $sin^{2}(\frac{5\alpha}{2})-sin^{2}(\frac{\alpha}{2})$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Let angle between $\vec{PQ}$ & $\vec{PS}$ is $\theta$ $cos\theta=\frac{\vec{PQ}.\vec{PS}}{|\vec{PQ}||\vec{PS}|}$ $cos\theta=\frac{0-1+0}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2}}$ $cos\theta=-\frac{1}{2}$ $\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ $\alpha=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{2}\text{So}\alpha=\frac{\pi}{6}$ $sin^{2}\frac{5\alpha}{2}-sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}=sin(\frac{5\alpha}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2})sin(\frac{5\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2})$ $=sin\frac{6\alpha}{2} \times sin\frac{4\alpha}{2}$ $=sin3\alpha \times sin2\alpha$ $=sin\frac{\pi}{2} \times sin\frac{\pi}{3}$ $=1 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let angle between $\vec{PQ}$ & $\vec{PS}$ is $\theta$

$cos\theta=\frac{\vec{PQ}.\vec{PS}}{|\vec{PQ}||\vec{PS}|}$

$cos\theta=\frac{0-1+0}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2}}$

$cos\theta=-\frac{1}{2}$

$\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}$

$\alpha=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{2}\text{So}\alpha=\frac{\pi}{6}$

$sin^{2}\frac{5\alpha}{2}-sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}=sin(\frac{5\alpha}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2})sin(\frac{5\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2})$

$=sin\frac{6\alpha}{2} \times sin\frac{4\alpha}{2}$

$=sin3\alpha \times sin2\alpha$

$=sin\frac{\pi}{2} \times sin\frac{\pi}{3}$

This means $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}-2\vec{c}$ are parallel vectors

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{b}-2\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{a} \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{b}=\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{c}-(1) \end{aligned}$

It is given that $|\vec{a}|=1,|b|=4$ and $|\vec{c}|=2$ , angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c},\theta=60^{\circ}$ .

$|b|^{2}=|\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{c}|^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|b|^{2}=\lambda^{2}|a|^{2}+4|c|^{2}+4\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda^{2}+4\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})=0$ .......(2)

Taking dot product with $\vec{c}$ in equation (1)

$\Rightarrow$ $4 \times 2 \times 1/2=\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})+2(2)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $4=\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})+8$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})=-4$

From (2) and (3)

$\lambda^{2}+4(-4)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda^{2}-16=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda= \pm 4$

from (3)

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-4/\lambda$

if $\lambda=4$ , then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-1$

if $\lambda=-4$ , then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=1$

$|\vec{a} \cdot c|=1$

questions.question_text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle such that $\vec{PQ}=-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{PR}=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k},a,b \in Z$ . Let S be the point on QR , which is equidistant from the lines PQ and PR . If $|\vec{PR}|=9$ and $\vec{PS}=\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ , then the value of $3a-4b$ is $____$
questions.question_html: Let $PQR$ be a triangle such that $\vec{PQ}=-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{PR}=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k},a,b \in Z$ . Let S be the point on QR , which is equidistant from the lines PQ and PR . If $|\vec{PR}|=9$ and $\vec{PS}=\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ , then the value of $3a-4b$ is $____$
questions.explanation_text: We are given that $|\vec{PR}|=9$ Using the distance formula for the vector $PR=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ : $\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+16=81$ $\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}+b^{2}=65$ The problem states that point $S$ lies on $QR$ and is equidistant from lines $PQ$ and $PR$ . In a triangle, the locus of points equidistant from two sides is the angle bisector. Therefore, $\vec{PS}$ is the internal angle bisector of $\angleQPR$ . For an angle bisector $\vec{PS}$ , it must be collinear with the sum of the unit vectors along the adjacent sides : $\vec{PS}=\lambda(\frac{\vec{PQ}}{|\vec{PQ}|}+\frac{\vec{PR}}{|\vec{PR}|})$ where $\lambda$ is a scalar constant. First, calculate $|\vec{PQ}|$ : $|\vec{PQ}|=\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3$ Now, set up the bisector equation : $\vec{PS}=\lambda(\frac{-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}}{3}+\frac{a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k}}{9})$ Multiply the first term by $\frac{3}{3}$ to get a common denominator: $\vec{PS}=\frac{\lambda}{9}((-6+a)\hat{i}+(-3+b)\hat{j}+(6-4)\hat{k})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{PS}=\frac{\lambda}{9}((a-6)\hat{i}+(b-3)\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$ We are given $\vec{PS}=\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Comparing the $\hat{k}$ -components: $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda}{9}(2)=2 \Rightarrow \lambda=9$ Substitute $\lambda=9$ into other components: For $\hat{i}$ : $a-6=1 \Rightarrow a=7$ For $\hat{j}$ : $b-3=-7 \Rightarrow b=-4$ Check against the constraint : $a^{2}+b^{2}=7^{2}+(-4)^{2}=49+16=65$ The values are consistent. value of $3a-4b$ : $3a-4b=3(7)-4(-4)$ $=21+16=𝟑𝟕$
questions.explanation_html:
We are given that $|\vec{PR}|=9$ Using the distance formula for the vector $PR=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ :

$\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+16=81$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}+b^{2}=65$

The problem states that point $S$ lies on $QR$ and is equidistant from lines $PQ$ and $PR$ . In a triangle, the locus of points equidistant from two sides is the angle bisector. Therefore, $\vec{PS}$ is the internal angle bisector of $\angleQPR$ .

For an angle bisector $\vec{PS}$ , it must be collinear with the sum of the unit vectors along the adjacent sides :

$\vec{PS}=\lambda(\frac{\vec{PQ}}{|\vec{PQ}|}+\frac{\vec{PR}}{|\vec{PR}|})$

where $\lambda$ is a scalar constant.

First, calculate $|\vec{PQ}|$ :

$|\vec{PQ}|=\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3$

Now, set up the bisector equation :

$\vec{PS}=\lambda(\frac{-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}}{3}+\frac{a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}-4\hat{k}}{9})$

Multiply the first term by $\frac{3}{3}$ to get a common denominator:

$\vec{PS}=\frac{\lambda}{9}((-6+a)\hat{i}+(-3+b)\hat{j}+(6-4)\hat{k})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{PS}=\frac{\lambda}{9}((a-6)\hat{i}+(b-3)\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$

We are given

$\vec{PS}=\hat{i}-7\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

Comparing the $\hat{k}$ -components:

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\lambda}{9}(2)=2 \Rightarrow \lambda=9$

Substitute $\lambda=9$ into other components:

For $\hat{i}$ :

$a-6=1 \Rightarrow a=7$

For $\hat{j}$ :

$b-3=-7 \Rightarrow b=-4$

Check against the constraint :

$a^{2}+b^{2}=7^{2}+(-4)^{2}=49+16=65$

The values are consistent. value of $3a-4b$ :

$3a-4b=3(7)-4(-4)$ $=21+16=𝟑𝟕$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\sqrt{7}\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{r}$ is a vector such that $\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ , then $|3\vec{r}|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Given $\vec{a}=\sqrt{7}\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0},\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ We have to find $|3\vec{r}|^{2}$ . From $\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$ note that $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=-(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$ So, $\vec{r} \times \vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ Hence, $(\vec{r}-\vec{b}) \times \vec{a}=0$ This means $\vec{r}-\vec{b}$ is parallel to $\vec{a}$ . Therefore, $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda$ . Now use the condition $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ Substitute $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$ : $(\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}) \cdot \vec{a}=0$ So, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}+\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})=0$ Now calculate these dot products. 1. Find $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ $\vec{b}=(0,1,2),\vec{a}=(\sqrt{7},1,-1)$ Thus, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=0 \cdot \sqrt{7}+1 \cdot 1+2 \cdot (-1)=1-2=-1$ 2. Find $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=(\sqrt{7})^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}=7+1+1=9$ Therefore, $-1+9\lambda=0$ So, $\lambda=\frac{1}{9}$ Hence, $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}$ Now find $|\vec{r}|^{2}$ . Using $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}$ we get $|\vec{r}|^{2}=|\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}|^{2}$ Expand: $|\vec{r}|^{2}=|\vec{b}|^{2}+\frac{1}{81}|\vec{a}|^{2}+\frac{2}{9}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$ Now, $|\vec{b}|^{2}=0^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}=5$ $|\vec{a}|^{2}=9$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=-1$ So, $|\vec{r}|^{2}=5+\frac{9}{81}+\frac{2}{9}(-1)$ $=5+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{2}{9}=5-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{44}{9}$ Therefore, $|3\vec{r}|^{2}=9|\vec{r}|^{2}=9 \cdot \frac{44}{9}=44$ So the correct answer is: $44$ Hence, Option A .
questions.explanation_html:
Given

$\vec{a}=\sqrt{7}\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

and

$\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0},\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$

We have to find $|3\vec{r}|^{2}$ .

From

$\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$

note that

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=-(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$

So,

$\vec{r} \times \vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$

Hence,

$(\vec{r}-\vec{b}) \times \vec{a}=0$

This means $\vec{r}-\vec{b}$ is parallel to $\vec{a}$ . Therefore,

$\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$

for some scalar $\lambda$ .

Now use the condition

$\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$

Substitute $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$ :

$(\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}) \cdot \vec{a}=0$

So,

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}+\lambda(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})=0$

Now calculate these dot products.

1. Find $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$

$\vec{b}=(0,1,2),\vec{a}=(\sqrt{7},1,-1)$

Thus,

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=0 \cdot \sqrt{7}+1 \cdot 1+2 \cdot (-1)=1-2=-1$

2. Find $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}$

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=(\sqrt{7})^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}=7+1+1=9$

Therefore,

$-1+9\lambda=0$

So,

$\lambda=\frac{1}{9}$

Hence,

$\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}$

Now find $|\vec{r}|^{2}$ .

Using

$\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}$

we get

$|\vec{r}|^{2}=|\vec{b}+\frac{1}{9}\vec{a}|^{2}$

Expand:

$|\vec{r}|^{2}=|\vec{b}|^{2}+\frac{1}{81}|\vec{a}|^{2}+\frac{2}{9}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$

Now,

$|\vec{b}|^{2}=0^{2}+1^{2}+2^{2}=5$

$|\vec{a}|^{2}=9$

$=5+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{2}{9}=5-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{44}{9}$

Therefore,

$|3\vec{r}|^{2}=9|\vec{r}|^{2}=9 \cdot \frac{44}{9}=44$

So the correct answer is:

$44$

Hence, Option A.

questions.explanation_text: We are given two unit vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ with an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ between them. This means: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}=1$ (since they are unit vectors) $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$ We need to find the number of values of $\lambda$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ for which the vectors $\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}$ and $3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b}$ are perpendicular, meaning their dot product is zero. Here’s how to solve the problem step by step: Set up the perpendicular condition by equating the dot product to zero: $(\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}) \cdot (3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b})=0.$ Expand the dot product using the distributive property: $\begin{aligned} (\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}) \cdot (3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b}) & =\lambda \cdot 3(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})-\lambda^{2}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})+2 \cdot 3(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a})-2\lambda(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}) \\ & =3\lambda-\lambda^{2}(\frac{1}{2})+6(\frac{1}{2})-2\lambda \\ & =3\lambda-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}+3-2\lambda. \end{aligned}$ Simplify the expression: $3\lambda-2\lambda=\lambda,$ so the equation becomes: $\lambda-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}+3=0.$ Multiply the entire equation by 2 to eliminate the fraction: $2\lambda-\lambda^{2}+6=0,$ which can be rearranged as: $-\lambda^{2}+2\lambda+6=0.$ Multiply both sides by -1 to get a standard quadratic form: $\lambda^{2}-2\lambda-6=0.$ Solve the quadratic equation using the quadratic formula: $\lambda=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4 \cdot 1 \cdot (-6)}}{2}=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4+24}}{2}=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{28}}{2}.$ Notice that: $\sqrt{28}=2\sqrt{7},$ thus: $\lambda=\frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{2}=1 \pm \sqrt{7}.$ Evaluate the solutions numerically: $\lambda=1+\sqrt{7} \approx 1+2.6458 \approx 3.6458,$ $\lambda=1-\sqrt{7} \approx 1-2.6458 \approx -1.6458.$ Check if the solutions are in the interval $[-1,3]$ : $1+\sqrt{7} \approx 3.6458$ is greater than 3. $1-\sqrt{7} \approx -1.6458$ is less than -1. Since neither value lies within the interval $[-1,3]$ , there are no valid values of $\lambda$ in that interval. Therefore, the number of values of $\lambda$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ is: 0
questions.explanation_html:
We are given two unit vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ with an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ between them. This means:

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}=1$ (since they are unit vectors)

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}$

We need to find the number of values of $\lambda$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ for which the vectors $\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}$ and $3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b}$ are perpendicular, meaning their dot product is zero.

Here’s how to solve the problem step by step:

Set up the perpendicular condition by equating the dot product to zero:

$(\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}) \cdot (3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b})=0.$

Expand the dot product using the distributive property:

$\begin{aligned} (\lambda\vec{a}+2\vec{b}) \cdot (3\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b}) & =\lambda \cdot 3(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})-\lambda^{2}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})+2 \cdot 3(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a})-2\lambda(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}) \\ & =3\lambda-\lambda^{2}(\frac{1}{2})+6(\frac{1}{2})-2\lambda \\ & =3\lambda-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}+3-2\lambda. \end{aligned}$

Simplify the expression:

$3\lambda-2\lambda=\lambda,$

so the equation becomes:

$\lambda-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}+3=0.$

Multiply the entire equation by 2 to eliminate the fraction:

$2\lambda-\lambda^{2}+6=0,$

which can be rearranged as:

$-\lambda^{2}+2\lambda+6=0.$

Multiply both sides by -1 to get a standard quadratic form:

$\lambda^{2}-2\lambda-6=0.$

Solve the quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$\lambda=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4 \cdot 1 \cdot (-6)}}{2}=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4+24}}{2}=\frac{2 \pm \sqrt{28}}{2}.$

Notice that:

$\sqrt{28}=2\sqrt{7},$

thus:

$\lambda=\frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{2}=1 \pm \sqrt{7}.$

Evaluate the solutions numerically:

$\lambda=1+\sqrt{7} \approx 1+2.6458 \approx 3.6458,$

$\lambda=1-\sqrt{7} \approx 1-2.6458 \approx -1.6458.$

Check if the solutions are in the interval $[-1,3]$ :

$1+\sqrt{7} \approx 3.6458$ is greater than 3.

$1-\sqrt{7} \approx -1.6458$ is less than -1.

Since neither value lies within the interval $[-1,3]$ , there are no valid values of $\lambda$ in that interval.

Therefore, the number of values of $\lambda$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ is:

0

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{Assuming Vertex}A\text{to be origin} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \vec{A}=\vec{a}_{1}=\vec{0} \\ & \vec{B}=\vec{a}_{1}+\vec{u}=\vec{u}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ & \vec{C}=\vec{a}_{1}+\vec{v}=\vec{v}=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-4\hat{k} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ One solving $\vec{A}=\vec{0},\vec{B}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{C}=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ , are the position vector of vertices $AB$ and $C$ respectively. $\begin{aligned} & \vec{G}=\frac{1}{3}(\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C})=\frac{1}{3}(\vec{0}+\vec{B}+\vec{C})=\frac{1}{3}(\vec{B}+\vec{C}) \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{G}=\frac{5}{3}\hat{i}-\frac{5}{3}\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ & \vec{AG}=\vec{G}-\vec{A}=\vec{G} \\ & |\vec{AG}|^{2}=(\frac{5}{3})^{2}+(\frac{5}{3})^{2}+(1)^{2}=\frac{25}{9}+\frac{25}{9}+1=\frac{50}{9}+1=\frac{59}{9} \\ & \vec{BC}=\vec{G}-\vec{B} \\ & \vec{B}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ & |\vec{BG}|^{2}=(\frac{1}{3})^{3}+(\frac{2}{3})^{2}+4=\frac{1}{9}+\frac{4}{9}+4=\frac{5}{9}+4=\frac{41}{9} \\ & \vec{CG}=\vec{G}-\vec{C} \\ & \vec{C}=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-4\hat{k} \\ & \vec{CG}|^{2}=(\frac{4}{3})^{2}+(\frac{7}{3})^{2}+9=\frac{16}{9}+\frac{49}{9}+9=\frac{65}{9}+9=\frac{65}{9}+\frac{81}{9}=\frac{146}{9} \end{aligned}$ $6(|\vec{AG}|^{2}+|\vec{BG}|^{2}+|\vec{CG}|^{2})=6 \cdot (\frac{59}{9}+\frac{41}{9}+\frac{146}{9})=6 \cdot \frac{246}{9}=164$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{c}$ be the projection vector of $\vec{b}=\lambda\hat{i}+4\hat{k},\lambda>0$ , on the vector $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ . If $|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7$ , then the area of the parallelogram formed by the vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is _________.
questions.explanation_text: To find the projection vector $\vec{c}$ of $\vec{b}=\lambda\hat{i}+4\hat{k}$ (where $\lambda>0$ ) onto vector $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ , we use the formula for the projection of a vector: $\vec{c}=(\frac{\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|^{2}})\vec{a}$ Calculate the dot product $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ : $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=(\lambda\hat{i}+4\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=\lambda \cdot 1+4 \cdot 2=\lambda+8$ Calculate the magnitude of $\vec{a}$ : $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3$ Now substitute to find $\vec{c}$ : $\vec{c}=(\frac{\lambda+8}{9})(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$ We know that the magnitude $|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7$ . Thus, substituting $\vec{c}$ in this equation, we resolve it to find $\lambda$ : $|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7 \Rightarrow (\lambda=4)$ This indicates that $\lambda$ has a value of 4. Next, calculating the area of the parallelogram formed by vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ involves finding the cross product $|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|$ : $\vec{b}=4\hat{i}+4\hat{k},\vec{c}=(\frac{12}{9})(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=(\frac{4}{3})\hat{i}+(\frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(\frac{8}{3})\hat{k}$ The cross product is: $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{ı} & \hat{ȷ} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{4}{3} & \frac{8}{3} & \frac{8}{3} \\ 4 & 0 & 4 \end{aligned}|$ Solving the determinant: $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=((\frac{8}{3} \times 4-0 \times \frac{8}{3})\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{3} \times 4-4 \times \frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(\frac{4}{3} \times 0-\frac{8}{3} \times 4)\hat{k})$ $=(\frac{32}{3}\hat{i}+0\hat{j}+(-\frac{32}{3})\hat{k})$ Then, the magnitude is calculated as: $|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=\sqrt{(\frac{32}{3})^{2}+0+(-\frac{32}{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{(\frac{32}{3})^{2}+(\frac{32}{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2048}{9}}$ $=\frac{\sqrt{2048}}{3}=\frac{16}{3} \times 3 \approx 16$ Therefore, the area of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is 16.

Calculate the dot product $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ :

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=(\lambda\hat{i}+4\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=\lambda \cdot 1+4 \cdot 2=\lambda+8$

Calculate the magnitude of $\vec{a}$ :

$|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3$

Now substitute to find $\vec{c}$ :

$\vec{c}=(\frac{\lambda+8}{9})(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$

We know that the magnitude $|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7$ . Thus, substituting $\vec{c}$ in this equation, we resolve it to find $\lambda$ :

$|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7 \Rightarrow (\lambda=4)$

This indicates that $\lambda$ has a value of 4.

Next, calculating the area of the parallelogram formed by vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ involves finding the cross product $|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|$ :

$\vec{b}=4\hat{i}+4\hat{k},\vec{c}=(\frac{12}{9})(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=(\frac{4}{3})\hat{i}+(\frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(\frac{8}{3})\hat{k}$

The cross product is:

$\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{ı} & \hat{ȷ} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{4}{3} & \frac{8}{3} & \frac{8}{3} \\ 4 & 0 & 4 \end{aligned}|$

Solving the determinant:

$\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=((\frac{8}{3} \times 4-0 \times \frac{8}{3})\hat{i}-(\frac{4}{3} \times 4-4 \times \frac{8}{3})\hat{j}+(\frac{4}{3} \times 0-\frac{8}{3} \times 4)\hat{k})$

$=(\frac{32}{3}\hat{i}+0\hat{j}+(-\frac{32}{3})\hat{k})$

Then, the magnitude is calculated as:

$|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=\sqrt{(\frac{32}{3})^{2}+0+(-\frac{32}{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{(\frac{32}{3})^{2}+(\frac{32}{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2048}{9}}$

$=\frac{\sqrt{2048}}{3}=\frac{16}{3} \times 3 \approx 16$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram formed by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is 16.

questions.explanation_text: To solve the problem, we begin by examining the vector $\vec{c}=3\hat{a}+6\hat{b}+9(\hat{a} \times \hat{b})$ . Let's calculate: $\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a}=3+6(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$ . $\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b}=3(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})+6$ . We need to find the value of $9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})-3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})$ . Substituting the expressions, we get: $9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})=9(3+6\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})=27+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$ $3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})=3(3\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+6)=9\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+18$ Therefore, $9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})-3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})=(27+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}))-(9\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+18)$ Simplifying, $=27-18+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})-9(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$ $=9+45(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$ Given $sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9}$ , and knowing that for unit vectors $cos\theta=\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}$ , we use the identity $(cos\theta)^{2}=1-(sin\theta)^{2}$ : $(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})^{2}=1-(\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9})^{2}$ $=1-\frac{65}{81}$ $=\frac{16}{81}$ Thus, $\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}=\frac{4}{9}$ . Substitute back into the equation: $9+45 \times \frac{4}{9}=9+20=29$ Therefore, the value is 29.
questions.explanation_html:
To solve the problem, we begin by examining the vector $\vec{c}=3\hat{a}+6\hat{b}+9(\hat{a} \times \hat{b})$ .

Let's calculate:

$\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a}=3+6(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$ .

$\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b}=3(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})+6$ .

We need to find the value of $9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})-3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})$ .

Substituting the expressions, we get:

$9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})=9(3+6\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})=27+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$

$3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})=3(3\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+6)=9\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+18$

Therefore,

$9(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{a})-3(\vec{c} \cdot \hat{b})=(27+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}))-(9\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}+18)$

Simplifying,

$=27-18+54(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})-9(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$

$=9+45(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})$

Given $sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9}$ , and knowing that for unit vectors $cos\theta=\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}$ , we use the identity $(cos\theta)^{2}=1-(sin\theta)^{2}$ :

$(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b})^{2}=1-(\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9})^{2}$

$=1-\frac{65}{81}$

$=\frac{16}{81}$

Thus, $\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b}=\frac{4}{9}$ .

Substitute back into the equation:

$9+45 \times \frac{4}{9}=9+20=29$

Therefore, the value is 29.

Expressing $\vec{b}-\vec{c}$ : Calculate $\vec{b}-\vec{c}=(3\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})-(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ . Calculate: $\vec{a}-\vec{b}=(-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$ Therefore, we can express $\hat{d}$ as: $\hat{d}=\frac{-2}{3}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{3}\hat{j}+\frac{2}{3}\hat{k}$ Solve for $\lambda$ and $\mu$ : Using the condition $\vec{c} \cdot \hat{d}=1$ : $\frac{-\lambda}{3}+\frac{2\mu}{3}=1$ Simplify to: $-\lambda+2\mu=3\text{...(i)}$ Since $\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ : $\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ Which gives: $\lambda+\mu=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-\mu$ Substitute $\lambda=-\mu$ into equation (i): $\mu+2\mu=3 \Rightarrow 3\mu=3 \Rightarrow \mu=1$ Therefore, $\lambda=-1$ . Substituting this into the equation, we get: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}+\vec{d}=-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}.$ Now, we take the dot product of both sides with $\vec{a}$ : $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})+\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=\vec{a} \cdot (-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}).$ Since the dot product $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ is zero (the dot product of any vector with the cross product of itself with another vector is zero), we have: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=-36+9+12=-15.$ Thus, the magnitude of $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}$ is: $|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}|=15.$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ & \vec{b}=((\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})) \times \hat{i}) \times \hat{i} \\ & \vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{aligned}| \\ & =\hat{i}(1)-\hat{j}(1)+\hat{k}(2-1) \\ & =\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & (\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})) \times \hat{i}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}| \\ & =\hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(-1)+\hat{k}(1) \\ & =\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $((\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times \hat{i}) \times \hat{i}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}|$ $\begin{aligned} & =\hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(-1)+\hat{k}(-1) \\ \vec{b}= & \hat{j}-\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}$ Square of projection $=2$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ & \vec{b}=((\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})) \times \hat{i}) \times \hat{i} \\ & \vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{aligned}| \\ & =\hat{i}(1)-\hat{j}(1)+\hat{k}(2-1) \\ & =\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & (\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j})) \times \hat{i}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}| \\ & =\hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(-1)+\hat{k}(1) \\ & =\hat{j}+\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$((\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times \hat{i}) \times \hat{i}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{aligned}|$

$\begin{aligned} & =\hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(-1)+\hat{k}(-1) \\ \vec{b}= & \hat{j}-\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$

$=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}$

Square of projection $=2$

questions.explanation_text: Area of quadrilateral $ABCD=$ area of $△ABC+$ area of $△ADC$ In $△ABC$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{AB}=4,8,-8 \\ & \vec{BC}=-2,-3,-4 \\ & \vec{AB} \times \vec{BC}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 8 & -8 \\ -2 & -3 & -4 \end{aligned}| \\ & =-56\hat{i}+32\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Area of $△ABC=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{BC}|$ $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{56^{2}+32^{2}+4^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4176}=\frac{12\sqrt{29}}{2}=6\sqrt{29} \end{aligned}$ In $△ADC=\vec{AD}=-2,-3,-4$ $\vec{DC}=4,8,-8$ $\vec{AD} \times \vec{DC}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & -3 & -4 \\ 4 & 8 & -8 \end{aligned}|$ $=56\hat{i}-32\hat{j}-4k$ $\text{Area of}\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AD} \times \vec{DC}|$ $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4176} \\ & =6\sqrt{29} \end{aligned}$ Area of $ABCD=6\sqrt{29}+6\sqrt{29}$ $=12\sqrt{29}$

Area of quadrilateral $ABCD=$ area of $△ABC+$ area of $△ADC$

In $△ABC$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{AB}=4,8,-8 \\ & \vec{BC}=-2,-3,-4 \\ & \vec{AB} \times \vec{BC}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 8 & -8 \\ -2 & -3 & -4 \end{aligned}| \\ & =-56\hat{i}+32\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Area of $△ABC=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB} \times \vec{BC}|$

$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{56^{2}+32^{2}+4^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4176}=\frac{12\sqrt{29}}{2}=6\sqrt{29} \end{aligned}$

In $△ADC=\vec{AD}=-2,-3,-4$

$\vec{DC}=4,8,-8$

$\vec{AD} \times \vec{DC}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -2 & -3 & -4 \\ 4 & 8 & -8 \end{aligned}|$

$=56\hat{i}-32\hat{j}-4k$

$\text{Area of}\frac{1}{2}|\vec{AD} \times \vec{DC}|$

$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4176} \\ & =6\sqrt{29} \end{aligned}$

Area of $ABCD=6\sqrt{29}+6\sqrt{29}$

$=12\sqrt{29}$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two vectors such that $|\vec{b}|=1$ and $|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|=2$ . Then $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: To find the value of $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}$ , we can use properties of vector operations and magnitudes. Given $|\vec{b}|=1$ and $|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|=2$ , let's break down the calculation step by step: Firstly, we observe that the cross product of two vectors $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ is orthogonal (perpendicular) to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}$ . This means that when we take the dot product of $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ with either $\vec{b}$ or $\vec{a}$ , the result will be zero due to the orthogonal property. Specifically, $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{b}=0$ (because $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}$ ) Next, to find the magnitude squared of the vector $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}$ , we apply the formula for the magnitude squared of a vector subtraction, which can be expressed as: $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|^{2}+|-\vec{b}|^{2}+2(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot (-\vec{b})$ Since $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{b}=0$ and $|-\vec{b}|=|\vec{b}|$ , the equation simplifies to: $=|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}$ Given that $|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|=2$ and $|\vec{b}|=1$ , substituting these values gives: $=2^{2}+1^{2}=4+1=5$ Therefore, the value of $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}$ is 5 .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the value of $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}$ , we can use properties of vector operations and magnitudes. Given $|\vec{b}|=1$ and $|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|=2$ , let's break down the calculation step by step:

Firstly, we observe that the cross product of two vectors $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ is orthogonal (perpendicular) to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}$ . This means that when we take the dot product of $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ with either $\vec{b}$ or $\vec{a}$ , the result will be zero due to the orthogonal property. Specifically,

$(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{b}=0$ (because $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}$ )

Next, to find the magnitude squared of the vector $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}$ , we apply the formula for the magnitude squared of a vector subtraction, which can be expressed as:

$|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|^{2}+|-\vec{b}|^{2}+2(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot (-\vec{b})$

Since $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{b}=0$ and $|-\vec{b}|=|\vec{b}|$ , the equation simplifies to:

$=|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}$

Given that $|\vec{b} \times \vec{a}|=2$ and $|\vec{b}|=1$ , substituting these values gives:

$=2^{2}+1^{2}=4+1=5$

Therefore, the value of $|(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-\vec{b}|^{2}$ is 5.

(i)} \\ & \bar{AB} \times \bar{AC}|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -7 \\ 6 & d & -2 \end{aligned}| \\ & =(7d-4)\hat{i}-40\hat{j}+(d-12)\hat{k}\text{... (ii)} \end{aligned}$ From (i) and (ii) $5d^{2}-8d-4=0$ $\Rightarrow d=\frac{-}{5}$ (Rejected) or $d=2$ Also, $\bar{AB}+\bar{BC}=\bar{AC}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow a+1=6 \Rightarrow a=5 \\ & b+2=d \Rightarrow b=0 \end{aligned}$ and $c-7=-2 \Rightarrow c=5$ $|\bar{AB}|=\sqrt{54},|\bar{AC}|=\sqrt{44},|\bar{BC}|=\sqrt{50}$ Largest side has length of $\sqrt{54}$ units

Area of triangle $ABC=15\sqrt{2}$

Our goal is to find $(14cos\theta)^{2}$ , where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ . Step 1. Use the Perpendicularity Condition Two vectors are perpendicular if their dot product is zero. So, we require: $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a}-\vec{b})=0.$ First, compute $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ : $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=(\hat{i}+3\hat{i})+(\lambda\hat{j}-\hat{j})+(-3\hat{k}+2\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-\hat{k}.$ $\vec{a}-\vec{b}=(\hat{i}-3\hat{i})+(\lambda\hat{j}+\hat{j})+(-3\hat{k}-2\hat{k})=-2\hat{i}+(\lambda+1)\hat{j}-5\hat{k}.$ Now, take their dot product: $(4\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot (-2\hat{i}+(\lambda+1)\hat{j}-5\hat{k})$ $=4(-2)+(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)+(-1)(-5)=-8+(\lambda^{2}-1)+5.$ $=\lambda^{2}-4.$ Setting the dot product to zero: $\lambda^{2}-4=0⟹\lambda^{2}=4.$ Since $\lambda>0$ , we have: $\lambda=2.$ Step 2. Compute $(14cos\theta)^{2}$ $(14cos\theta)^{2}=(14 \cdot \frac{-5}{14})^{2}=(-5)^{2}=25.$ Final Answer The value of $(14cos\theta)^{2}$ is: $25.$
questions.explanation_html:
We are given the vectors

$\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}-3\hat{k}\text{and}\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k},$

with $\lambda>0$ , and we are told that the vectors $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ are perpendicular. Our goal is to find $(14cos\theta)^{2}$ , where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ .

Step 1. Use the Perpendicularity Condition

Two vectors are perpendicular if their dot product is zero. So, we require:

$(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a}-\vec{b})=0.$

First, compute $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ :

$\vec{a}+\vec{b}=(\hat{i}+3\hat{i})+(\lambda\hat{j}-\hat{j})+(-3\hat{k}+2\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-\hat{k}.$

$\vec{a}-\vec{b}=(\hat{i}-3\hat{i})+(\lambda\hat{j}+\hat{j})+(-3\hat{k}-2\hat{k})=-2\hat{i}+(\lambda+1)\hat{j}-5\hat{k}.$

Now, take their dot product:

$(4\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot (-2\hat{i}+(\lambda+1)\hat{j}-5\hat{k})$

$=4(-2)+(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)+(-1)(-5)=-8+(\lambda^{2}-1)+5.$

$=\lambda^{2}-4.$

Setting the dot product to zero:

$\lambda^{2}-4=0⟹\lambda^{2}=4.$

Since $\lambda>0$ , we have:

$\lambda=2.$

Step 2. Find the Angle Between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$

Now that we know $\lambda=2$ , the vectors become:

$\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k},\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}.$

The cosine of the angle $\theta$ between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by:

$cos\theta=\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{‖\vec{a}‖‖\vec{b}‖}.$

Calculate $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ :

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=(1)(3)+(2)(-1)+(-3)(2)=3-2-6=-5.$

Calculate the magnitudes:

$‖\vec{a}‖=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{1+4+9}=\sqrt{14}.$

$‖\vec{b}‖=\sqrt{3^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{9+1+4}=\sqrt{14}.$

Thus,

$cos\theta=\frac{-5}{\sqrt{14} \cdot \sqrt{14}}=\frac{-5}{14}.$

Step 3. Compute $(14cos\theta)^{2}$

$(14cos\theta)^{2}=(14 \cdot \frac{-5}{14})^{2}=(-5)^{2}=25.$

Final Answer

The value of $(14cos\theta)^{2}$ is:

$25.$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+k \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+2k \\ \\ & \vec{c}=4\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}k \\ \\ & \vec{b} \times \vec{a}=\vec{c} \times \vec{a} \\ \\ & (\vec{b}-\vec{c}) \times \vec{a}=0 \\ \\ & \vec{b}-\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{\alpha} \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\vec{c}+\lambda\vec{\alpha} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & -\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+2k=(4\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}k)+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+k) \\ \\ & \lambda+4=-1 \Rightarrow \lambda=-5 \\ \\ & \lambda+c_{2}=-8 \Rightarrow c_{2}=-3 \\ \\ & \lambda+c_{3}=2 \Rightarrow c_{3}=7 \\ \\ & \vec{c}=4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+7k \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & cos\theta=\frac{12-12+7}{\sqrt{26} \cdot \sqrt{74}}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{26} \cdot \sqrt{74}}=\frac{7}{2\sqrt{481}} \\ \\ & tan^{2}\theta=\frac{625 \times 3}{49} \\ \\ & [tan^{2}\theta]=38 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+k \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+2k \\ \\ & \vec{c}=4\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}k \\ \\ & \vec{b} \times \vec{a}=\vec{c} \times \vec{a} \\ \\ & (\vec{b}-\vec{c}) \times \vec{a}=0 \\ \\ & \vec{b}-\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{\alpha} \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\vec{c}+\lambda\vec{\alpha} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & -\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+2k=(4\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}k)+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+k) \\ \\ & \lambda+4=-1 \Rightarrow \lambda=-5 \\ \\ & \lambda+c_{2}=-8 \Rightarrow c_{2}=-3 \\ \\ & \lambda+c_{3}=2 \Rightarrow c_{3}=7 \\ \\ & \vec{c}=4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+7k \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & cos\theta=\frac{12-12+7}{\sqrt{26} \cdot \sqrt{74}}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{26} \cdot \sqrt{74}}=\frac{7}{2\sqrt{481}} \\ \\ & tan^{2}\theta=\frac{625 \times 3}{49} \\ \\ & [tan^{2}\theta]=38 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k},\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k},x \in R$ <?p> $\text{also,}\vec{b}+\vec{c}=(x+2)\hat{i}+6\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\vec{d}\text{is the unit vector in the direction of}\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ $\begin{aligned} & |\vec{b}+\vec{c}|=\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}+6^{2}+2^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}} \\ & \vec{d}=\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}}}\hat{i}+\frac{6}{\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}}}\hat{j}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}}}\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=1 \\ & \frac{x+2+6-2}{\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}}}=1 \\ & x+6=\sqrt{40+(x+2)^{2}} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & (x+6)^{2}=40+(x+2)^{2} \\ & x^{2}+36+12x=40+x^{2}+4+4x \\ & 8x=8 \\ & \Rightarrow x=1 \\ & (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c}=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}] \\ & =⎡⎣⎢\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & -5 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{aligned}⎤⎦⎥ \\ & =1(12+10)-1(6+5)+1(4-4) \\ & =22-11=11 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: A vector in the direction of the required line can be obtained by cross product of $\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =-9\hat{i}-9\hat{j}+9\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Required line $\begin{aligned} & \vec{r}=(5\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+3\hat{k})+\lambda^{'}(-9\hat{i}-9\hat{j}+9\hat{k}) \\ \\ & \vec{r}=(5\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+3\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$ Now distance of $(0,2,-2)$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{P.V. of}P \equiv (5+\lambda)\hat{i}+(\lambda-4)\hat{j}+(3-\lambda)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{AP}=(5+\lambda)\hat{i}+(\lambda-6)\hat{j}+(5-\lambda)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{AP} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})=0 \\ \\ & 5+\lambda+\lambda-6-5+\lambda=0 \\ \\ & \lambda=2 \\ \\ & |\vec{AP}|=\sqrt{49+16+9} \\ \\ & |\vec{AP}|=\sqrt{74} \end{aligned}$

(i) Angle between $\hat{u}$ and $\vec{p}_{2}=\frac{\pi}{3}$ $\hat{u} \cdot \vec{p}_{2}=|\hat{u}| \cdot |\vec{p}_{2}|cos\frac{\pi}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow y+z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ...... (ii) Angle between $\hat{u}$ and $\vec{p}_{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ $\hat{u} \cdot \vec{p}_{3}=|\hat{u}| \cdot |\vec{p}_{3}|cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-1}{2} \Rightarrow x+y=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ..... (iii) from equation (i), (ii) and (iii) we get $x=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}y=0z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Thus}\hat{u}-\vec{v}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k} \\ & \hat{u}-\vec{v}=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} \\ & \therefore |\hat{u}-\vec{v}|^{2}=(\sqrt{\frac{4}{2}+\frac{1}{2}})^{2}=\frac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$

Unit vector $\hat{u}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{p}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k},\vec{p}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k} \\ & \vec{p}_{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} \end{aligned}$

$\hat{u} \cdot \vec{p}_{1}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}=0$

$\Rightarrow x+z=0$ ...... (i)

Angle between $\hat{u}$ and $\vec{p}_{2}=\frac{\pi}{3}$

$\hat{u} \cdot \vec{p}_{2}=|\hat{u}| \cdot |\vec{p}_{2}|cos\frac{\pi}{3}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow y+z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ...... (ii)

Angle between $\hat{u}$ and $\vec{p}_{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$

$\hat{u} \cdot \vec{p}_{3}=|\hat{u}| \cdot |\vec{p}_{3}|cos\frac{2\pi}{3}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-1}{2} \Rightarrow x+y=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ..... (iii)

from equation (i), (ii) and (iii) we get

$x=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}y=0z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Thus}\hat{u}-\vec{v}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{k} \\ & \hat{u}-\vec{v}=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} \\ & \therefore |\hat{u}-\vec{v}|^{2}=(\sqrt{\frac{4}{2}+\frac{1}{2}})^{2}=\frac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$

If $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=13$ , then $(24-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c})$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation_text: Let $\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+13\hat{k}=\vec{u}$ Given $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b}+\vec{c})+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{u}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \vec{a} \times \vec{b}+\vec{a} \times \vec{c}+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{u} \\ (\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times c=\vec{u}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b} \end{aligned}$ Taking cross product with $\vec{a}$ on both sides $\vec{a} \times ((\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times \vec{c})=\vec{a} \times (\vec{u}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ $\Rightarrow \vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}^{2}+\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})=13(\vec{a}+\vec{b})-\vec{a} \times \vec{u}+(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{a}-\vec{a}^{2}\vec{b}$ ${ \because \vec{a}.\vec{c}=13}$ Putting the values, $\vec{c}=(-1,-1,3)$ $\vec{b}.\vec{c}=-22$ $\Rightarrow 24-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=46$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+13\hat{k}=\vec{u}$

Given $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b}+\vec{c})+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{u}$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \vec{a} \times \vec{b}+\vec{a} \times \vec{c}+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{u} \\ (\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times c=\vec{u}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b} \end{aligned}$

Taking cross product with $\vec{a}$ on both sides

$\vec{a} \times ((\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times \vec{c})=\vec{a} \times (\vec{u}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$

$\Rightarrow \vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a}^{2}+\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})=13(\vec{a}+\vec{b})-\vec{a} \times \vec{u}+(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{a}-\vec{a}^{2}\vec{b}$ ${ \because \vec{a}.\vec{c}=13}$

Putting the values, $\vec{c}=(-1,-1,3)$

$\vec{b}.\vec{c}=-22$

$\Rightarrow 24-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=46$

If $\alpha$ is a positive real number, then $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Let three vectors , $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k},\vec{b}=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{c}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ form a triangle such that $\vec{c}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ and the area of the triangle is $5\sqrt{6}$ . If $\alpha$ is a positive real number, then $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: To solve this, let's start with the given vector equation: $\vec{c}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ Given vectors are: $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ Then, the vector $\vec{c}$ is: $\vec{c}=(\alpha\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$ $\vec{c}=(\alpha-5)\hat{i}+(4-3)\hat{j}+(2-4)\hat{k}$ $\vec{c}=(\alpha-5)\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ The area of the triangle formed by vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by the magnitude of the cross product of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ , divided by 2: $\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=5\sqrt{6}$ This implies: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=10\sqrt{6}$ Let's find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ : $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \alpha & 4 & 2 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(4 \cdot 4-2 \cdot 3)-\hat{j}(\alpha \cdot 4-2 \cdot 5)+\hat{k}(\alpha \cdot 3-4 \cdot 5)$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\hat{i}(16-6)-\hat{j}(4\alpha-10)+\hat{k}(3\alpha-20)$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\hat{i}(10)-\hat{j}(4\alpha-10)+\hat{k}(3\alpha-20)$ Magnitude of $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ : $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=\sqrt{10^{2}+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}}$ We know: $\sqrt{10^{2}+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}}=10\sqrt{6}$ Squaring both sides: $100+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}=600$ $100+16\alpha^{2}-80\alpha+100+9\alpha^{2}-120\alpha+400=600$ $25\alpha^{2}-200\alpha+600=600$ $25\alpha^{2}-200\alpha=0$ $\alpha^{2}-8\alpha=0$ $\alpha(\alpha-8)=0$ Since $\alpha$ is a positive real number: $\alpha=8$ Then, the vector $\vec{c}$ is: $\vec{c}=(8-5)\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\vec{c}=3\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ Magnitude squared of $\vec{c}$ is: $|\vec{c}|^{2}=3^{2}+1^{2}+(-2)^{2}$ $|\vec{c}|^{2}=9+1+4$ $|\vec{c}|^{2}=14$ Therefore, the correct option is: Option A: 14
questions.explanation_html:
To solve this, let's start with the given vector equation:

$\vec{c}=\vec{a}-\vec{b}$

Given vectors are:

$\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

Then, the vector $\vec{c}$ is:

$\vec{c}=(\alpha\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+2\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$

$\vec{c}=(\alpha-5)\hat{i}+(4-3)\hat{j}+(2-4)\hat{k}$

$\vec{c}=(\alpha-5)\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

The area of the triangle formed by vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by the magnitude of the cross product of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ , divided by 2:

$\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=5\sqrt{6}$

This implies:

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=10\sqrt{6}$

Let's find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ :

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \alpha & 4 & 2 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}(4 \cdot 4-2 \cdot 3)-\hat{j}(\alpha \cdot 4-2 \cdot 5)+\hat{k}(\alpha \cdot 3-4 \cdot 5)$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\hat{i}(16-6)-\hat{j}(4\alpha-10)+\hat{k}(3\alpha-20)$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\hat{i}(10)-\hat{j}(4\alpha-10)+\hat{k}(3\alpha-20)$

Magnitude of $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ :

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=\sqrt{10^{2}+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}}$

We know:

$\sqrt{10^{2}+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}}=10\sqrt{6}$

Squaring both sides:

$100+(4\alpha-10)^{2}+(3\alpha-20)^{2}=600$

$100+16\alpha^{2}-80\alpha+100+9\alpha^{2}-120\alpha+400=600$

$25\alpha^{2}-200\alpha+600=600$

$25\alpha^{2}-200\alpha=0$

$\alpha^{2}-8\alpha=0$

$\alpha(\alpha-8)=0$

Since $\alpha$ is a positive real number:

$\alpha=8$

Then, the vector $\vec{c}$ is:

$\vec{c}=(8-5)\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$\vec{c}=3\hat{i}+1\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

Magnitude squared of $\vec{c}$ is:

$|\vec{c}|^{2}=3^{2}+1^{2}+(-2)^{2}$

$|\vec{c}|^{2}=9+1+4$

$|\vec{c}|^{2}=14$

Therefore, the correct option is:

Option A: 14
