questions.question_text: Consider three vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ . Let $|\vec{a}|=2,|\vec{b}|=3$ and $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ . If $\alpha \in [0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , then the minimum value of $27|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Consider three vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ . Let $|\vec{a}|=2,|\vec{b}|=3$ and $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ . If $\alpha \in [0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , then the minimum value of $27|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c} \\ & |\vec{a}|=2,|\vec{b}|=3 \end{aligned}$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=0$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=0$ $\begin{aligned} & |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=|\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{a}|^{2}-2\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a} \\ & =4+|\vec{c}|^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & |\vec{a}|=|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{b}|sin\alpha|\vec{c}| \\ & \Rightarrow sin\alpha|\vec{c}|=\frac{2}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow sin^{2}\alpha=\frac{4}{9|\vec{c}|^{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow |\vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{4}{9sin^{2}\alpha} \\ & \Rightarrow |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=4+\frac{4}{9sin^{2}\alpha} \end{aligned}$ For $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}$ to be minimum for $\alpha \in [0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$ $\begin{aligned} sin\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 27|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=27[4+\frac{4.4}{9.3}] \\ =27[\frac{124}{27}]=124 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c} \\ & |\vec{a}|=2,|\vec{b}|=3 \end{aligned}$

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=0$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=0$

$\begin{aligned} & |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=|\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{a}|^{2}-2\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a} \\ & =4+|\vec{c}|^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & |\vec{a}|=|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{b}|sin\alpha|\vec{c}| \\ & \Rightarrow sin\alpha|\vec{c}|=\frac{2}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow sin^{2}\alpha=\frac{4}{9|\vec{c}|^{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow |\vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{4}{9sin^{2}\alpha} \\ & \Rightarrow |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=4+\frac{4}{9sin^{2}\alpha} \end{aligned}$

For $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}$ to be minimum for $\alpha \in [0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$

$\begin{aligned} sin\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 27|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=27[4+\frac{4.4}{9.3}] \\ =27[\frac{124}{27}]=124 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let a unit vector which makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with $2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with $\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ be $\vec{C}$ . Then $\vec{C}+(-\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\hat{k})$ is:
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\vec{C}=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k} \\ & (a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k})=1 \times 3 \times \frac{1}{2} \\ & 2a+2b-c=\frac{3}{2}\text{... (1)} \\ & (a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}-\hat{k})=1 \times \sqrt{2} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & a-c=1\text{... (2)} \\ & a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=1\text{... (3)} \end{aligned}$ Solving (1), (2) and (3) $\begin{aligned} & a+2b=\frac{1}{2} \\ & a^{2}+b^{2}+(a-1)^{2}=1 \\ & 2a^{2}-2a+b^{2}=0 \\ & 2a^{2}-2a+(\frac{2a-1}{4})^{2}=0 \\ & 32a^{2}-32a+4a^{2}-4a+1=0 \\ & 36a^{2}-36a+1=0 \\ & a=\frac{36 \pm \sqrt{(36)^{2}-4(36)}}{2 \times 36} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ & b=\frac{1-2a}{4} \Rightarrow b=\frac{1 \pm \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}-1}{4} \\ & = \mp \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ & C=-\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & C+(\frac{-1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\hat{k}) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{2}\hat{k} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\vec{C}=a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k} \\ & (a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \cdot (2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k})=1 \times 3 \times \frac{1}{2} \\ & 2a+2b-c=\frac{3}{2}\text{... (1)} \\ & (a\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+c\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}-\hat{k})=1 \times \sqrt{2} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & a-c=1\text{... (2)} \\ & a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=1\text{... (3)} \end{aligned}$

Solving (1), (2) and (3)

$\begin{aligned} & a+2b=\frac{1}{2} \\ & a^{2}+b^{2}+(a-1)^{2}=1 \\ & 2a^{2}-2a+b^{2}=0 \\ & 2a^{2}-2a+(\frac{2a-1}{4})^{2}=0 \\ & 32a^{2}-32a+4a^{2}-4a+1=0 \\ & 36a^{2}-36a+1=0 \\ & a=\frac{36 \pm \sqrt{(36)^{2}-4(36)}}{2 \times 36} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ & b=\frac{1-2a}{4} \Rightarrow b=\frac{1 \pm \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}-1}{4} \\ & = \mp \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ & C=-\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & C+(\frac{-1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\hat{k}) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\hat{i}-\frac{1}{2}\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $S$ be the set of all $(\lambda,\mu)$ for which the vectors $\lambda\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k},\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ , where $\lambda-\mu=5$ , are coplanar, then $\underset{(\lambda,\mu) \in S}{\sum}80(\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $S$ be the set of all $(\lambda,\mu)$ for which the vectors $\lambda\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k},\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ , where $\lambda-\mu=5$ , are coplanar, then $\underset{(\lambda,\mu) \in S}{\sum}80(\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Given condition for coplanarity For three vectors to be coplanar, their scalar triple product must be zero. We have the vectors A, B, and C, and we know the given relation between λ and μ: $A=\lambda\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $B=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$ $C=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ Scalar triple product condition: $[A,B,C]=A \cdot (B \times C)=0$ Step 2: Calculate the cross product of B and C $B \times C=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & \mu \\ 3 & -4 & 5 \end{aligned}|$ $B \times C=(10+4\mu)\hat{i}-(5-3\mu)\hat{j}-10\hat{k}$ Step 3: Calculate the scalar triple product and apply the coplanarity condition $[A,B,C]=A \cdot (B \times C)=\lambda(10+4\mu)-1(5-3\mu)+1(-10)=0$ Step 4: Substitute the given relation between λ and μ
Given that: $\lambda-\mu=5$ From the coplanarity condition, we have: $4\lambda\mu+10\lambda-3\mu=5$ Now, substitute λ in terms of μ: $4(5+\mu)\mu+10(5+\mu)-3\mu=5$ Step 5: Solve for μ and λ Simplify the equation and solve for μ: $4\mu^{2}+27\mu+45=0$ Factor the equation: $(4\mu+15)(\mu+3)=0$ So, the two possible values for μ are: $\mu=-3,\frac{-15}{4}$ For each value of μ, find the corresponding value of λ using the given relation: $\lambda=\mu+5$ So, we get the values for λ: $\lambda=2,\frac{5}{4}$ Step 6: Calculate the sum Now, we need to find the sum: $\underset{(\lambda,\mu) \in S}{\sum}80(\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2})$ Substitute the values of λ and μ, and simplify: $80[(2^{2}+(-3)^{2})+(\frac{5}{4})^{2}+(\frac{-15}{4})^{2}]=80[13+\frac{25}{16}+\frac{225}{16}]$ $=80[13+\frac{250}{16}]=10 \times 229$ $=2290$ So, the correct answer is 2290 (Option D).
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Given condition for coplanarity

For three vectors to be coplanar, their scalar triple product must be zero. We have the vectors A, B, and C, and we know the given relation between λ and μ:

$A=\lambda\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$B=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$

$C=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$

Scalar triple product condition:

$[A,B,C]=A \cdot (B \times C)=0$

Step 2: Calculate the cross product of B and C

$B \times C=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & \mu \\ 3 & -4 & 5 \end{aligned}|$

$B \times C=(10+4\mu)\hat{i}-(5-3\mu)\hat{j}-10\hat{k}$

Step 3: Calculate the scalar triple product and apply the coplanarity condition

$[A,B,C]=A \cdot (B \times C)=\lambda(10+4\mu)-1(5-3\mu)+1(-10)=0$

Step 4: Substitute the given relation between λ and μ Given that:

$\lambda-\mu=5$

From the coplanarity condition, we have:

$4\lambda\mu+10\lambda-3\mu=5$

Now, substitute λ in terms of μ:

$4(5+\mu)\mu+10(5+\mu)-3\mu=5$

Step 5: Solve for μ and λ

Simplify the equation and solve for μ:

$4\mu^{2}+27\mu+45=0$

Factor the equation:

$(4\mu+15)(\mu+3)=0$

So, the two possible values for μ are:

$\mu=-3,\frac{-15}{4}$

For each value of μ, find the corresponding value of λ using the given relation:

$\lambda=\mu+5$

So, we get the values for λ:

$\lambda=2,\frac{5}{4}$

Step 6: Calculate the sum

Now, we need to find the sum:

$\underset{(\lambda,\mu) \in S}{\sum}80(\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2})$

Substitute the values of λ and μ, and simplify:

$80[(2^{2}+(-3)^{2})+(\frac{5}{4})^{2}+(\frac{-15}{4})^{2}]=80[13+\frac{25}{16}+\frac{225}{16}]$

$=80[13+\frac{250}{16}]=10 \times 229$

$=2290$

So, the correct answer is 2290 (Option D).

questions.question_text: Let O be the origin and the position vector of the point P be $-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . If the position vectors of the points A, B and C are $-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k},2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ respectively, then the projection of the vector $\vec{OP}$ on a vector perpendicular to the vectors $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ is :
questions.question_html: Let O be the origin and the position vector of the point P be $-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . If the position vectors of the points A, B and C are $-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k},2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ respectively, then the projection of the vector $\vec{OP}$ on a vector perpendicular to the vectors $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, the position vector of point P is : $\vec{OP}=-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ Position vectors of points A, B, and C are : $\vec{OA}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ $\vec{OB}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\vec{OC}=-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ Now, vectors $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ can be calculated as : $\vec{AB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OA}$ $=(2+2)\hat{i}+(4-1)\hat{j}-(-2+3)\hat{k}$ $=4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\vec{AC}=\vec{OC}-\vec{OA}$ $=(-4+2)\hat{i}+(2-1)\hat{j}-(-1+3)\hat{k}$ $=-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} \text{Now,}\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(5)+\hat{j}(-2-8)+\hat{k}(4+6) \\ \\ & =5\hat{i}-10\hat{j}+10\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{OP}=-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ To find the projection of $\vec{OP}$ onto $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ , we need to find the dot product between $\vec{OP}$ and the normalized vector $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ . First, find the magnitude of $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ : $|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}|=\sqrt{5^{2}+(-10)^{2}+10^{2}}$ $=\sqrt{25+100+100}$ $=\sqrt{225}$ $=15$ The projection of vector $\vec{OP}$ onto a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ (which is $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ ) is given by : $\frac{\vec{OP} \cdot (\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC})}{|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}|}$ = $\frac{(-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \cdot (5\hat{i}-10\hat{j}+10\hat{k})}{\sqrt{25+100+100}}$ $=\frac{-5+20+30}{15}$ $=\frac{45}{15}=3$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, the position vector of point P is : $\vec{OP}=-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

Position vectors of points A, B, and C are :

$\vec{OA}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$

$\vec{OB}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$\vec{OC}=-4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

Now, vectors $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ can be calculated as :

$\vec{AB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OA}$

$=(2+2)\hat{i}+(4-1)\hat{j}-(-2+3)\hat{k}$

$=4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

$\vec{AC}=\vec{OC}-\vec{OA}$

$=(-4+2)\hat{i}+(2-1)\hat{j}-(-1+3)\hat{k}$

$=-2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} \text{Now,}\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(5)+\hat{j}(-2-8)+\hat{k}(4+6) \\ \\ & =5\hat{i}-10\hat{j}+10\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{OP}=-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

To find the projection of $\vec{OP}$ onto $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ , we need to find the dot product between $\vec{OP}$ and the normalized vector $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ .

First, find the magnitude of $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ :

$|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}|=\sqrt{5^{2}+(-10)^{2}+10^{2}}$

$=\sqrt{25+100+100}$

$=\sqrt{225}$

$=15$

The projection of vector $\vec{OP}$ onto a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ (which is $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ ) is given by :

$\frac{\vec{OP} \cdot (\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC})}{|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}|}$

= $\frac{(-\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) \cdot (5\hat{i}-10\hat{j}+10\hat{k})}{\sqrt{25+100+100}}$

$=\frac{-5+20+30}{15}$

$=\frac{45}{15}=3$

$\alpha\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+13\hat{k},6\hat{i}+11\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$

and $\frac{9}{2}\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}-8\hat{k}$ are collinear.

So, $\frac{\alpha-6}{6-\frac{9}{2}}=\frac{10-11}{11-\beta}=\frac{13-11}{11+8}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{2(\alpha-6)}{3}=\frac{-1}{11-\beta}=\frac{2}{19} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}(\alpha-6)=\frac{2}{19} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 19\alpha-114=3 \Rightarrow 19\alpha=117 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{117}{19} \end{aligned}$

And, $\frac{-1}{11-\beta}=\frac{2}{19}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow -19=22-2\beta \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\beta=41 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{41}{2} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore (19\alpha-6\beta)^{2}=(19 \times \frac{117}{19}-\frac{6 \times 41}{2})^{2} \\ \\ & =(117-123)^{2}=36 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text:
Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=-\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ .

If $\vec{d}$ is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=18$ , then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=-\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{d}$ is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=18$ , then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given vectors : $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ $\vec{c}=-\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ Since $\vec{d}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , its direction is given by their cross product : $\vec{d}=\lambda(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ $\begin{aligned} \vec{b} \times \vec{c} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & 4 & 3 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(-6+8)-\hat{j}(3-2)+\hat{k}(4-2)=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Thus, $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ Given this, $\vec{d}$ can be expressed as : $\vec{d}=\lambda(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$ Using the given condition that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=18$ : $(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}) \cdot \lambda(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=18$ $\Rightarrow 2\lambda(2)-3\lambda(1)+4\lambda(2)=18$ $\Rightarrow \lambda(4+8-3)=18$ $\Rightarrow 9\lambda=18$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=2$ So, $\vec{d}=4\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ Now, using the identity : $|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}|\vec{d}|^{2}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d})^{2}$ Given $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{29}$ and $|\vec{d}|=\sqrt{4^{2}+(-2)^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{16+4+16}=\sqrt{36}=6$ Using your corrected calculations : $|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}=29 \times 36-18^{2}=1044-324=720$
questions.explanation_html:
Given vectors :

$\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

$\vec{c}=-\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

Since $\vec{d}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , its direction is given by their cross product :

$\vec{d}=\lambda(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$

$\begin{aligned} \vec{b} \times \vec{c} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & 4 & 3 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\hat{i}(-6+8)-\hat{j}(3-2)+\hat{k}(4-2)=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Thus, $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

Given this, $\vec{d}$ can be expressed as :

$\vec{d}=\lambda(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$

Using the given condition that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d}=18$ :

$(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}) \cdot \lambda(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=18$

$\Rightarrow 2\lambda(2)-3\lambda(1)+4\lambda(2)=18$

$\Rightarrow \lambda(4+8-3)=18$

$\Rightarrow 9\lambda=18$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=2$

So, $\vec{d}=4\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

Now, using the identity :

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}|\vec{d}|^{2}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d})^{2}$

Given $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{29}$

and $|\vec{d}|=\sqrt{4^{2}+(-2)^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{16+4+16}=\sqrt{36}=6$

Using your corrected calculations :

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{d}|^{2}=29 \times 36-18^{2}=1044-324=720$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{a}.\vec{b}=1$ and $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ . Then $\vec{a}-6\vec{b}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=(\hat{i}-\hat{j})$ Taking cross product with $\vec{a}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=\vec{a} \times (\hat{i}-\hat{j}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})\vec{a}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}-3\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\vec{a}-6\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}-6\vec{b}=3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Let $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ be parallel to $\vec{\alpha}$ and $\vec{\beta}_{2}$ be perpendicular to $\vec{\alpha}$ . If $\vec{\beta}=\vec{\beta}_{1}+\vec{\beta}_{2}$ , then the value of $5\vec{\beta}_{2}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{\alpha}=4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{\beta}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ . Let $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ be parallel to $\vec{\alpha}$ and $\vec{\beta}_{2}$ be perpendicular to $\vec{\alpha}$ . If $\vec{\beta}=\vec{\beta}_{1}+\vec{\beta}_{2}$ , then the value of $5\vec{\beta}_{2}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{\beta}_{1}=\lambda\vec{\alpha}$ Now $\vec{\beta}_{2}=\vec{\beta}-\vec{\beta}_{1}$ $\begin{aligned} & =(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k})-\lambda(4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =(1-4\lambda)\hat{i}+(2-3\lambda)\hat{j}-(5\lambda+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2} \cdot \vec{\alpha}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(1-4\lambda)+3(2-3\lambda)-5(5\lambda+4)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4-16\alpha+6-9\lambda-25\lambda-20=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 50\lambda=-10 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-1}{5} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2}=(1+\frac{4}{5})\hat{i}+(2+\frac{3}{5})\hat{j}-(-1+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2}=\frac{9}{5}\hat{i}+\frac{13}{5}\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & 5\vec{\beta}_{2}=9\hat{i}+13\hat{j}-15\hat{k} \\ \\ & 5\vec{\beta}_{2} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=9+13-15=7 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{\beta}_{1}=\lambda\vec{\alpha}$

Now $\vec{\beta}_{2}=\vec{\beta}-\vec{\beta}_{1}$

$\begin{aligned} & =(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-4\hat{k})-\lambda(4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =(1-4\lambda)\hat{i}+(2-3\lambda)\hat{j}-(5\lambda+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2} \cdot \vec{\alpha}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4(1-4\lambda)+3(2-3\lambda)-5(5\lambda+4)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4-16\alpha+6-9\lambda-25\lambda-20=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 50\lambda=-10 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-1}{5} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2}=(1+\frac{4}{5})\hat{i}+(2+\frac{3}{5})\hat{j}-(-1+4)\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{\beta}_{2}=\frac{9}{5}\hat{i}+\frac{13}{5}\hat{j}-3\hat{k} \\ \\ & 5\vec{\beta}_{2}=9\hat{i}+13\hat{j}-15\hat{k} \\ \\ & 5\vec{\beta}_{2} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=9+13-15=7 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{v}=\alpha\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k},\vec{w}=2\alpha\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{u}$ be a vector such that $|\vec{u}|=\alpha>0$ . If the minimum value of the scalar triple product $[\begin{aligned} \vec{u} & \vec{v} & \vec{w} \end{aligned}]$ is $-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$ , and $|\vec{u} \cdot \hat{i}|^{2}=\frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are coprime natural numbers, then $m+n$ is equal to ____________.
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{v}=\alpha\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k},\vec{w}=2\alpha\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{u}$ be a vector such that $|\vec{u}|=\alpha>0$ . If the minimum value of the scalar triple product $[\begin{aligned} \vec{u} & \vec{v} & \vec{w} \end{aligned}]$ is $-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$ , and $|\vec{u} \cdot \hat{i}|^{2}=\frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are coprime natural numbers, then $m+n$ is equal to ____________.
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \alpha & 2 & -3 \\ 2\alpha & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-5\alpha\hat{j}-3\alpha\hat{k}$ $[\begin{aligned} \vec{u} & \vec{v} & \vec{w} \end{aligned}]=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$ $=|\vec{u}||\vec{v} \times \vec{w}| \times cos\theta$ $=\alpha\sqrt{34\alpha^{2}+1}cos\theta$ $[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{w}]_{min}=-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$ $\alpha\sqrt{34\alpha^{2}+1} \times (-1)=-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$ (taking $cos\theta=1$ ) $\Rightarrow \alpha=10$ $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=\hat{i}-50\hat{j}-30\hat{k}$ $cos\theta=-1 \Rightarrow \vec{u}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}$ $\vec{u}=-|\vec{u}| \cdot \frac{\vec{v} \times \vec{w}}{|\vec{v} \times \vec{w}|}=\frac{-10(\hat{i}-50\hat{j}-30\hat{k})}{\sqrt{3401}}$ $|\vec{u} \cdot \hat{i}|^{2}=|\frac{-10}{\sqrt{3401}}|^{2}=\frac{100}{3401}=\frac{m}{n}$ $m+n=3501$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \alpha & 2 & -3 \\ 2\alpha & 1 & -1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-5\alpha\hat{j}-3\alpha\hat{k}$

$[\begin{aligned} \vec{u} & \vec{v} & \vec{w} \end{aligned}]=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$

$=|\vec{u}||\vec{v} \times \vec{w}| \times cos\theta$

$=\alpha\sqrt{34\alpha^{2}+1}cos\theta$

$[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{w}]_{min}=-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$

$\alpha\sqrt{34\alpha^{2}+1} \times (-1)=-\alpha\sqrt{3401}$

(taking $cos\theta=1$ )

$\Rightarrow \alpha=10$

$\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=\hat{i}-50\hat{j}-30\hat{k}$

$cos\theta=-1 \Rightarrow \vec{u}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}$

$\vec{u}=-|\vec{u}| \cdot \frac{\vec{v} \times \vec{w}}{|\vec{v} \times \vec{w}|}=\frac{-10(\hat{i}-50\hat{j}-30\hat{k})}{\sqrt{3401}}$

$|\vec{u} \cdot \hat{i}|^{2}=|\frac{-10}{\sqrt{3401}}|^{2}=\frac{100}{3401}=\frac{m}{n}$

$m+n=3501$

Let the position vectors of four points $A,B,C$ and $D$ be $\vec{a}-\vec{b}+\vec{c},\lambda\vec{a}-3\vec{b}+4\vec{c},-\vec{a}+2\vec{b}-3\vec{c}$ and $2\vec{a}-4\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ respectively. If $\vec{AB},\vec{AC}$ and $\vec{AD}$ are coplanar, then $\lambda$ is equal to __________.

If $\vec{AB},\vec{AC}$ and $\vec{AD}$ are coplanar, then $\lambda$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $\bar{AB}=(\lambda-1)\bar{a}-2\bar{b}+3\bar{c}$ $\bar{AC}=2\bar{a}+3\bar{b}-4\bar{c}$ $\bar{AD}=\bar{a}-3\bar{b}+5\bar{c}$ $|\begin{aligned} \lambda-1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -3 & 5 \end{aligned}|=0$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda-1)(15-12)+2(-10+4)+3(6-3)=0$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda-1)=1 \Rightarrow \lambda=2$

$\bar{AB}=(\lambda-1)\bar{a}-2\bar{b}+3\bar{c}$

$\bar{AC}=2\bar{a}+3\bar{b}-4\bar{c}$

$\bar{AD}=\bar{a}-3\bar{b}+5\bar{c}$

$\Rightarrow (\lambda-1)=1 \Rightarrow \lambda=2$

questions.question_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral. If $E$ and $F$ are the mid points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively and $(\vec{AB}-\vec{BC})+(\vec{AD}-\vec{DC})=k\vec{FE}$ , then $k$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral. If $E$ and $F$ are the mid points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively and $(\vec{AB}-\vec{BC})+(\vec{AD}-\vec{DC})=k\vec{FE}$ , then $k$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let the position vectors of $A,B,C,$ and $D$ be $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},$ and $\vec{d}$ , respectively. Then the position vector of $E$ is: $\vec{E}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2}$ And the position vector of $F$ is: $\vec{F}=\frac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}$ Now, we are given the equation: $(\vec{AB}-\vec{BC})+(\vec{AD}-\vec{DC})=k\vec{FE}$ We can rewrite this equation using the position vectors: $(\vec{b}-\vec{a}-(\vec{c}-\vec{b}))+(\vec{d}-\vec{a}-(\vec{c}-\vec{d}))=k(\vec{E}-\vec{F})$ Simplifying the equation, we get: $(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=\frac{k}{2}(2\vec{E}-2\vec{F})$ Now substitute $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{F}$ expressions we found earlier: $(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=\frac{k}{2}(2(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2})-2(\frac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}))$ Simplifying the equation: $(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=-\frac{k}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{d}-\vec{a}-\vec{c})$ Since both sides of the equation are equal: $k=-4$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the position vectors of $A,B,C,$ and $D$ be $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},$ and $\vec{d}$ , respectively.

Then the position vector of $E$ is:

$\vec{E}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2}$

And the position vector of $F$ is:

$\vec{F}=\frac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}$

Now, we are given the equation:

$(\vec{AB}-\vec{BC})+(\vec{AD}-\vec{DC})=k\vec{FE}$

We can rewrite this equation using the position vectors:

$(\vec{b}-\vec{a}-(\vec{c}-\vec{b}))+(\vec{d}-\vec{a}-(\vec{c}-\vec{d}))=k(\vec{E}-\vec{F})$

Simplifying the equation, we get:

$(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=\frac{k}{2}(2\vec{E}-2\vec{F})$

Now substitute $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{F}$ expressions we found earlier:

$(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=\frac{k}{2}(2(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{c}}{2})-2(\frac{\vec{b}+\vec{d}}{2}))$

Simplifying the equation:

$(2\vec{b}-2\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+2\vec{d})=-\frac{k}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{d}-\vec{a}-\vec{c})$

Since both sides of the equation are equal:

$k=-4$

questions.question_text: Let $a,b,c$ be three distinct real numbers, none equal to one. If the vectors $a\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+c\hat{k}$ are coplanar, then $\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $a,b,c$ be three distinct real numbers, none equal to one. If the vectors $a\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\hat{i}+b\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+c\hat{k}$ are coplanar, then $\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $|\begin{aligned} a & 1 & 1 \\ \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ \\ 1 & 1 & c \end{aligned}|=0$ $C_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}-C_{1},C_{3} \rightarrow C_{3}-C_{1}$ $\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} a & 1-a & 1-a \\ 1 & b-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & c-1 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & a(b-1)(c-1)-(1-a)(c-1)+(1-a)(1-b)=0 \\ \\ & a(1-b)(1-c)+(1-a)(1-c)+(1-a)(1-b)=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -1+\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=1 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$|\begin{aligned} a & 1 & 1 \\ \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ \\ 1 & 1 & c \end{aligned}|=0$

$C_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}-C_{1},C_{3} \rightarrow C_{3}-C_{1}$

$\begin{aligned} & |\begin{aligned} a & 1-a & 1-a \\ 1 & b-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & c-1 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & a(b-1)(c-1)-(1-a)(c-1)+(1-a)(1-b)=0 \\ \\ & a(1-b)(1-c)+(1-a)(1-c)+(1-a)(1-b)=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -1+\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=1 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}$ be a non-zero vector parallel to the line of intersection of the two planes described by $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ . If $\theta$ is the angle between the vector $\vec{a}$ and the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=6$ , then the ordered pair $(\theta,|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}$ be a non-zero vector parallel to the line of intersection of the two planes described by $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ . If $\theta$ is the angle between the vector $\vec{a}$ and the vector $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=6$ , then the ordered pair $(\theta,|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: We have, $\vec{a}$ is non-zero vector parallel to the line of intersection of the two planes described by $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ . Let $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are the normal vector to the plane $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ , respectively. $\begin{aligned} & n_{1}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & n_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}=\lambda|n_{1} \times n_{2}| \end{aligned}$ [ $\because a$ is parallel to line of intersection of both planes] $\begin{aligned} & =\lambda|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\lambda(-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$ $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=6[Given]$ $\lambda(0+4+2)=6$ $\lambda=1$ $\begin{aligned} \therefore \vec{a} & =-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ cos\theta & =\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{4+4}\sqrt{4+4+1}} \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$ $\therefore \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\begin{aligned} \vec{a} \times \vec{b} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| & =\sqrt{4+16+16}=6 \\ \\ \text{Hence,}(\theta,|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|) & =(\frac{\pi}{4},6) \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have, $\vec{a}$ is non-zero vector parallel to the line of intersection of the two planes described by $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ .

Let $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are the normal vector to the plane $\hat{i}+\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ , respectively.

$\begin{aligned} & n_{1}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & n_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a}=\lambda|n_{1} \times n_{2}| \end{aligned}$

[ $\because a$ is parallel to line of intersection of both planes]

$\begin{aligned} & =\lambda|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =\lambda(-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \end{aligned}$

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=6[Given]$

$\lambda(0+4+2)=6$

$\lambda=1$

$\begin{aligned} \therefore \vec{a} & =-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \\ \\ cos\theta & =\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{4+4}\sqrt{4+4+1}} \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\begin{aligned} \vec{a} \times \vec{b} & =|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \end{aligned}| \\ \\ & =2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| & =\sqrt{4+16+16}=6 \\ \\ \text{Hence,}(\theta,|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|) & =(\frac{\pi}{4},6) \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: An arc PQ of a circle subtends a right angle at its centre O. The mid point of the arc PQ is R. If $\vec{OP}=\vec{u},\vec{OR}=\vec{v}$ , and $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$ , then $\alpha,\beta^{2}$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.question_html: An arc PQ of a circle subtends a right angle at its centre O. The mid point of the arc PQ is R. If $\vec{OP}=\vec{u},\vec{OR}=\vec{v}$ , and $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$ , then $\alpha,\beta^{2}$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.explanation_text: An arc $PQ$ of a circle subtends a right angle at its centre $O$ . The mid-point of an $arcPQ$ is $R$ . So, $PR=RQ$ Also given that, $\vec{OP}=\vec{u},\vec{OR}=\vec{v}$ , and $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$ Let $\vec{OP}=\vec{u}$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{OQ}=\vec{q}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v} \\ \\ & \vec{OR}=\vec{v} \end{aligned}$ Clearly, $\vec{q}=\hat{j}$ $\vec{u}=\hat{i},\vec{v}=\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$ Now, given, $\vec{q}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & \hat{j}=\alpha(\hat{i})+\beta(\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}) \\ \\ \Rightarrow & \hat{j}=i(\alpha+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}})+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} \end{aligned}$ On comparing both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} \alpha+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}=0\text{and}\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha=-\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}} \therefore \beta=\sqrt{2} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha=-1,\beta^{2}=2 \end{aligned}$ Now, $\alpha$ and $\beta^{2}$ are roots of the quadratic equation is $x^{2}-x-2=0$
questions.explanation_html:
An arc $PQ$ of a circle subtends a right angle at its centre $O$ . The mid-point of an $arcPQ$ is $R$ . So, $PR=RQ$

Also given that, $\vec{OP}=\vec{u},\vec{OR}=\vec{v}$ , and $\vec{OQ}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$



Let $\vec{OP}=\vec{u}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{OQ}=\vec{q}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v} \\ \\ & \vec{OR}=\vec{v} \end{aligned}$

Clearly, $\vec{q}=\hat{j}$

$\vec{u}=\hat{i},\vec{v}=\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$

Now, given, $\vec{q}=\alpha\vec{u}+\beta\vec{v}$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & \hat{j}=\alpha(\hat{i})+\beta(\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}) \\ \\ \Rightarrow & \hat{j}=i(\alpha+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}})+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{j} \end{aligned}$

On comparing both sides, we get

$\begin{aligned} \alpha+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}=0\text{and}\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha=-\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{2}} \therefore \beta=\sqrt{2} \\ \\ \Rightarrow \alpha=-1,\beta^{2}=2 \end{aligned}$

Now, $\alpha$ and $\beta^{2}$ are roots of the quadratic equation is $x^{2}-x-2=0$

questions.question_text: Let the vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ represent three coterminous edges of a parallelopiped of volume V. Then the volume of the parallelopiped, whose coterminous edges are represented by $\vec{a},\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ and $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ represent three coterminous edges of a parallelopiped of volume V. Then the volume of the parallelopiped, whose coterminous edges are represented by $\vec{a},\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ and $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given that the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped formed by the vectors $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ is represented by the scalar triple product $[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]$ , which is the determinant of the 3 x 3 matrix with vectors $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ as its rows (or columns). When the vectors representing the coterminous edges of the parallelepiped are $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}$ , the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped is represented by : $\begin{aligned} & V=[\vec{a},\vec{b}+\vec{c},\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}] \\ \\ & =|\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{aligned}|[\begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} & \vec{c} \end{aligned}] \\ \\ & =1(3-2)[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}] \\ \\ & =[\begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} & \vec{c} \end{aligned}]=V \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped formed by the vectors $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ is represented by the scalar triple product $[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]$ , which is the determinant of the 3 x 3 matrix with vectors $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ as its rows (or columns).

When the vectors representing the coterminous edges of the parallelepiped are $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}$ , the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped is represented by :

$\begin{aligned} & V=[\vec{a},\vec{b}+\vec{c},\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}] \\ \\ & =|\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{aligned}|[\begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} & \vec{c} \end{aligned}] \\ \\ & =1(3-2)[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}] \\ \\ & =[\begin{aligned} \vec{a} & \vec{b} & \vec{c} \end{aligned}]=V \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\lambda \in ℝ,\vec{a}=\lambda\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}-\lambda\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ . If $((\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})=8\hat{i}-40\hat{j}-24\hat{k}$ , then $|\lambda(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $\lambda \in ℝ,\vec{a}=\lambda\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}-\lambda\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ .

If $((\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})=8\hat{i}-40\hat{j}-24\hat{k}$ ,

then $|\lambda(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $(\vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})+\vec{b} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})$ $=(\vec{a}(\vec{a}.\vec{b})-\vec{b}(\vec{a}.\vec{a})+\vec{a}(\vec{b}.\vec{b})-\vec{b}(\vec{a}.\vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})$ $=(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})-(\vec{a}.\vec{a})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}-\vec{b} \times \vec{b})+(\vec{b}.\vec{b})(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}-\vec{b} \times \vec{b})$ $=(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-(\vec{a}.\vec{a})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})+(\vec{b}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$ $=(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})(\vec{b}.\vec{b}-\vec{a}.\vec{a})$ $=(5\vec{b} \times \vec{a})(5+\lambda^{2}-13-\lambda^{2})$ $=8(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \lambda & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -\lambda & 2 \end{aligned}|$ $=\hat{i}(4-3\lambda)-\hat{j}(2\lambda+3)+\hat{k}(-\lambda^{2}-2)$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=1$ $|\vec{a} \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})+\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})|^{2}$ $=|2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|^{2}=4.35=140$
questions.explanation_html:
$(\vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})+\vec{b} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})$

$=(\vec{a}(\vec{a}.\vec{b})-\vec{b}(\vec{a}.\vec{a})+\vec{a}(\vec{b}.\vec{b})-\vec{b}(\vec{a}.\vec{b})) \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})$

$=(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})-(\vec{a}.\vec{a})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}-\vec{b} \times \vec{b})+(\vec{b}.\vec{b})(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}-\vec{a} \times \vec{b})-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}-\vec{b} \times \vec{b})$

$=(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-(\vec{a}.\vec{a})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})+(\vec{b}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$

$=(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})(\vec{b}.\vec{b}-\vec{a}.\vec{a})$

$=(5\vec{b} \times \vec{a})(5+\lambda^{2}-13-\lambda^{2})$

$=8(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \lambda & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & -\lambda & 2 \end{aligned}|$

$=\hat{i}(4-3\lambda)-\hat{j}(2\lambda+3)+\hat{k}(-\lambda^{2}-2)$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=1$

$|\vec{a} \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})+\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}-\vec{b})|^{2}$

$=|2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|^{2}=4.35=140$

questions.question_text: If $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{c}=7\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{r} \times \vec{b}+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{r}.\vec{a}=0$ . Then $\vec{r}.\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k},\vec{c}=7\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},\vec{r} \times \vec{b}+\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{r}.\vec{a}=0$ . Then $\vec{r}.\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $(\vec{r}-\vec{c}) \times \vec{b}=0$ $\vec{r}=\lambda\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda\vec{b}.\vec{a}+\vec{c}.\vec{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda(3)+(7+8)=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=-5$ $\vec{r}=5\vec{b}+\vec{c}$ $=-5\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-5\hat{k}+(7\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$ $=2\hat{i}-8\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{r}.\vec{c}=17+24-4=34$
questions.explanation_html:
$(\vec{r}-\vec{c}) \times \vec{b}=0$

$\vec{r}=\lambda\vec{b}+\vec{c}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda\vec{b}.\vec{a}+\vec{c}.\vec{a}=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda(3)+(7+8)=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=-5$

$\vec{r}=5\vec{b}+\vec{c}$

$=-5\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-5\hat{k}+(7\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$

$=2\hat{i}-8\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{r}.\vec{c}=17+24-4=34$

questions.question_html:
Let PQR be a triangle. The points A, B and C are on the sides QR, RP and PQ respectively such that

$\frac{QA}{AR}=\frac{RB}{BP}=\frac{PC}{CQ}=\frac{1}{2}$ . Then $\frac{Area(\Delta PQR)}{Area(\Delta ABC)}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let the position vector of $P,Q,R$ be $\vec{0},\vec{a},\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ Position vector of $A=\frac{2\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3},$ Position vector of $B=\frac{2\vec{b}}{3}$ and Position vector of $C=\frac{\vec{a}}{3}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{AB}=\frac{2\vec{b}}{3}-(\frac{2\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3})=\frac{\vec{b}}{3}-\frac{2\vec{a}}{3}=\frac{\vec{b}-2\vec{a}}{3} \\ \\ & \vec{CA}=\frac{2\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3}-\frac{\vec{a}}{3}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3} \\ \\ & \text{Area of}△PQR=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{PQ} \times \vec{PR}|=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \\ \\ & \text{Area of}△ABC=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{CA} \times \vec{AB}| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}|(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3}) \times (\frac{\vec{b}-2\vec{a}}{3})|=\frac{1}{2}|\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{3}| \\ \\ & \therefore \frac{\text{Area}(△PQR)}{\text{Area}(△ABC)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}{\frac{1}{2}|\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{3}|}=3\text{sq. units} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{b}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ and $|\vec{b}|^{2}=50$ , then $|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}|$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{b}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ and $|\vec{b}|^{2}=50$ , then $|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}|$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: Given that $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ , we can find the magnitudes of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ : $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$ $|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-3)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{22}$ We know that the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors is equal to the product of the magnitudes of the vectors and the sine of the angle between them : $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|sin\theta$ Plugging in the known values : $\sqrt{11}=\sqrt{50}\sqrt{22}sin\theta$ Solving for the sine of the angle between the vectors : $sin\theta=\frac{1}{10}$ Now we can find $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}$ using the formula : $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$ We have the dot product $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|cos\theta$ , and we can use the relationship between sine and cosine: $cos\theta=\sqrt{1-sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}$ . Substitute the values into the formula : $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=50+22+2\sqrt{50}\sqrt{22}\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}=72+66$ Finally, we need to find the absolute value of the difference : $|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}|=|72-(72+66)|=66$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that $\vec{a}=\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$ , we can find the magnitudes of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ :

$|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{11}$

$|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-3)^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{22}$

We know that the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors is equal to the product of the magnitudes of the vectors and the sine of the angle between them :

$|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|sin\theta$

Plugging in the known values :

$\sqrt{11}=\sqrt{50}\sqrt{22}sin\theta$

Solving for the sine of the angle between the vectors :

$sin\theta=\frac{1}{10}$

Now we can find $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}$ using the formula :

$|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$

We have the dot product $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|cos\theta$ , and we can use the relationship between sine and cosine: $cos\theta=\sqrt{1-sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}$ .

Substitute the values into the formula :

$|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=50+22+2\sqrt{50}\sqrt{22}\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}=72+66$

Finally, we need to find the absolute value of the difference :

$|72-|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}|=|72-(72+66)|=66$

questions.question_html: $A(2,6,2),B(-4,0,\lambda),C(2,3,-1)$ and $D(4,5,0),|\lambda| \le 5$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ . If its area is 18 square units, then $5-6\lambda$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & A(2,6,2)B(-4,0,\lambda),C(2,3,-1)D(4,5,0) \\ \\ & \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{BD} \times \vec{AC}|=18 \\ \\ & \vec{AC} \times \vec{BD}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & j & k \\ \\ 0 & -3 & -3 \\ \\ 8 & 5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =(3\lambda+15)\hat{i}-\hat{j}(-24)+\hat{k}(-24) \\ \\ & \vec{AC} \times \vec{BD}=(3\lambda+15)\hat{i}+24\hat{j}-24\hat{k} \\ \\ & =\sqrt{(3\lambda+15)^{2}+(24)^{2}+(24)^{2}}=36 \\ \\ & =\lambda^{2}+10\lambda+9=0 \\ \\ & =\lambda=-1,-9 \\ \\ & |\lambda| \le 5 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \\ \\ & 5-6\lambda=5-6(-1)=11 \end{aligned}$

Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}) \times \vec{c}=\vec{0},\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-17$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-20$ . Then $|\vec{c} \times (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$ is equal to :

Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}) \times \vec{c}=\vec{0},\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-17$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-20$ . Then $|\vec{c} \times (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: The given vectors are : $\vec{a}=\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ We are given that $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}) \times \vec{c}=0$ which implies $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=0$ . So, $\vec{c}$ is in the direction of $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ . Let's denote $\vec{c}=\alpha(\vec{a}+\vec{b})$ . Substituting values for $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ , we get : $\vec{c}=\alpha((\lambda+3)\hat{i}+\hat{k})$ From the conditions $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-17$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-20$ , we can form two equations : $\alpha\lambda(\lambda+3)-\alpha=-17\text{and}\alpha(3\lambda+9+2)=-20.$ By solving the above equations, we find $\alpha=-1$ and $\lambda=3$ . Substituting these values back into $\vec{c}$ gives $\vec{c}=-6\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ . Next, we need to find $|\vec{c} \times (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$ . This simplifies to : $|\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$ Calculate the cross product $\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ which gives : $=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -6 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}$ Finally, the square of the magnitude of this vector is: $|\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}=(1)^{2}+3^{2}+(-6)^{2}=1+9+36=46.$
questions.explanation_html:
The given vectors are :

$\vec{a}=\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

We are given that $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}) \times \vec{c}=0$ which implies $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=0$ . So, $\vec{c}$ is in the direction of $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ .

Let's denote $\vec{c}=\alpha(\vec{a}+\vec{b})$ .

Substituting values for $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ , we get :

$\vec{c}=\alpha((\lambda+3)\hat{i}+\hat{k})$

From the conditions $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-17$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-20$ , we can form two equations :

$\alpha\lambda(\lambda+3)-\alpha=-17\text{and}\alpha(3\lambda+9+2)=-20.$

By solving the above equations, we find $\alpha=-1$ and $\lambda=3$ .

Substituting these values back into $\vec{c}$ gives $\vec{c}=-6\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ .

Next, we need to find $|\vec{c} \times (\lambda\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$ .

This simplifies to :

$|\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}$

Calculate the cross product $\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ which gives :

$=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -6 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}$

Finally, the square of the magnitude of this vector is:

$|\vec{c} \times (3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})|^{2}=(1)^{2}+3^{2}+(-6)^{2}=1+9+36=46.$

So, $[\begin{aligned} \vec{u}_{1} & \vec{u}_{2} & \vec{u}_{3} \end{aligned}]=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 1 & 1 & a \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ c & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 1(b-1)-1(1-c)+a(1-bc)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow b-1-1+c+a-abc=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a+b+c-2=abc...........(i) \end{aligned}$ Also, $[\begin{aligned} \vec{v}_{1} & \vec{v}_{2} & \vec{v}_{3} \end{aligned}]=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} a+b & c & c \\ a & b+c & a \\ b & b & c+a \end{aligned}|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow (a+b)[bc+ba+c^{2}+ca-ab]-c[ac+a^{2}-ab] \\ \\ & +c[ab-b^{2}-bc]=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow abc+ac^{2}+a^{2}c+b^{2}c+bc^{2}+abc-ac^{2}-a^{2}c \\ \\ & +abc+abc-b^{2}c-bc^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4abc=0 \Rightarrow abc=0 \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \text{So,}a+b+c-2=0[from(i)] \\ \\ \Rightarrow a+b+c=2 \end{aligned} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6(a+b+c)=12 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} a+b & c & c \\ a & b+c & a \\ b & b & c+a \end{aligned}|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow (a+b)[bc+ba+c^{2}+ca-ab]-c[ac+a^{2}-ab] \\ \\ & +c[ab-b^{2}-bc]=0 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{OA}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{OB}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{OC}=(a+1)\hat{i}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ and $\vec{OD}=9\hat{i}+(a-8)\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{AB}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{AC}=a\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \text{and}\vec{AD}=8\hat{i}+(a-6)\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Since, given point are coplanar $\begin{aligned} & \therefore [\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}]=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ a & 2 & -1 \\ 8 & a-6 & 3 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 1(6+a-6)+1(3a+8)+1(a^{2}-6a-16)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a+3a+8+a^{2}-6a-16=0 \Rightarrow a^{2}-2a-8=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-4a+2a-8=0 \Rightarrow a(a-4)+2(a-4)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (a-4)(a+2)=0 \Rightarrow a=4,-2 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Sum of all values of}a=4-2=2 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{OA}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{OB}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{OC}=(a+1)\hat{i}+2\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

and $\vec{OD}=9\hat{i}+(a-8)\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{AB}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{AC}=a\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \text{and}\vec{AD}=8\hat{i}+(a-6)\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Since, given point are coplanar

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore [\vec{AB},\vec{AC},\vec{AD}]=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ a & 2 & -1 \\ 8 & a-6 & 3 \end{aligned}|=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 1(6+a-6)+1(3a+8)+1(a^{2}-6a-16)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a+3a+8+a^{2}-6a-16=0 \Rightarrow a^{2}-2a-8=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-4a+2a-8=0 \Rightarrow a(a-4)+2(a-4)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (a-4)(a+2)=0 \Rightarrow a=4,-2 \\ \\ & \therefore \text{Sum of all values of}a=4-2=2 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=4\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{c}.(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})+25=0,\vec{c}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=4$ , and projection of $\vec{c}$ on $\vec{a}$ is 1, then the projection of $\vec{c}$ on $\vec{b}$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: $[\begin{aligned} \vec{c} & \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned}]=-25$ Let $\vec{c}=l\hat{i}+n\hat{j}+n\hat{k}$ $|\begin{aligned} l & m & n \\ 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -4 & 5 \end{aligned}|=-25$ $\Rightarrow 3l-4m-5n=-5$ ..... (i) $\vec{c}.(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=4$ $\Rightarrow l+m+n=4$ ..... (ii) $\frac{\vec{c}.\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}=1 \Rightarrow \vec{c}.\vec{a}=5$ $\Rightarrow 4l+3m=5$ ...... (iii) Using (i), (ii) and (iii) $l=2,m=-1,n=3$ Now, $\frac{\vec{c}.\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}=\frac{25}{5\sqrt{2}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore$ Option (2) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
$[\begin{aligned} \vec{c} & \vec{a} & \vec{b} \end{aligned}]=-25$

Let $\vec{c}=l\hat{i}+n\hat{j}+n\hat{k}$

questions.question_text: The vector $\vec{a}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ is rotated through a right angle, passing through the y-axis in its way and the resulting vector is $\vec{b}$ . Then the projection of $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ on $\vec{c}=5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ is :
questions.question_html: The vector $\vec{a}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ is rotated through a right angle, passing through the y-axis in its way and the resulting vector is $\vec{b}$ . Then the projection of $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ on $\vec{c}=5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: First, we write $\vec{b}$ as a linear combination of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{j}$ since $\vec{b}$ is a rotation of $\vec{a}$ about the y-axis. $\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu\hat{j}=-\lambda\hat{i}+(2\lambda+\mu\hat{j})+\lambda\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}$ is orthogonal to $\vec{a}$ due to the right angle rotation, so $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ . This implies : $\begin{aligned} & (-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot (-\lambda\hat{i}+(2\lambda+\mu)\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k})=0 \\ \\ & \lambda+2(2\lambda+\mu)+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow 6\lambda+2\mu=0 \Rightarrow \mu+3\lambda=0 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{a}-3\lambda\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})-3\lambda\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ The magnitude of $\vec{b}$ is the same as the magnitude of $\vec{a}$ because a rotation doesn't change the magnitude of a vector. This gives us : $|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{3}|\lambda|=\sqrt{6}[ \because |a|=\sqrt{6}] \Rightarrow |\lambda|=\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow \lambda \ne \sqrt{2}$ as for this value of $\lambda$ angle between $b$ and $y$ -axis is not acute. Therefore $\lambda=-\sqrt{2}$ Thus, we have : $\vec{b}=-\sqrt{2}(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})=\sqrt{2}\hat{i}+\sqrt{2}\hat{j}-\sqrt{2}\hat{k}$ Then, we find the vector $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ : $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}=3(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}\hat{i}+\sqrt{2}\hat{j}-\sqrt{2}\hat{k})$ $=-3\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}+2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}=-\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ The projection of this vector onto $\vec{c}$ is given by the dot product divided by the magnitude of $\vec{c}$ : $\frac{(-\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot (5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k})}{\sqrt{5^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}}}=\frac{-5+32+3}{\sqrt{50}}=\frac{30}{5\sqrt{2}}=3\sqrt{2}$ So the projection of $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ onto $\vec{c}$ is $3\sqrt{2}$ which is option D.
questions.explanation_html:
First, we write $\vec{b}$ as a linear combination of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{j}$ since $\vec{b}$ is a rotation of $\vec{a}$ about the y-axis.

$\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu\hat{j}=-\lambda\hat{i}+(2\lambda+\mu\hat{j})+\lambda\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}$ is orthogonal to $\vec{a}$ due to the right angle rotation, so $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}=0$ .

This implies :

$\begin{aligned} & (-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot (-\lambda\hat{i}+(2\lambda+\mu)\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k})=0 \\ \\ & \lambda+2(2\lambda+\mu)+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow 6\lambda+2\mu=0 \Rightarrow \mu+3\lambda=0 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{a}-3\lambda\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})-3\lambda\hat{j}=\lambda(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$

The magnitude of $\vec{b}$ is the same as the magnitude of $\vec{a}$ because a rotation doesn't change the magnitude of a vector. This gives us :

$|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{3}|\lambda|=\sqrt{6}[ \because |a|=\sqrt{6}] \Rightarrow |\lambda|=\sqrt{2} \Rightarrow \lambda \ne \sqrt{2}$

as for this value of $\lambda$ angle between $b$ and $y$ -axis is not acute.

Therefore $\lambda=-\sqrt{2}$

Thus, we have :

$\vec{b}=-\sqrt{2}(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})=\sqrt{2}\hat{i}+\sqrt{2}\hat{j}-\sqrt{2}\hat{k}$

Then, we find the vector $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ :

$3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}=3(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}\hat{i}+\sqrt{2}\hat{j}-\sqrt{2}\hat{k})$

$=-3\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}+2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}=-\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

The projection of this vector onto $\vec{c}$ is given by the dot product divided by the magnitude of $\vec{c}$ :

$\frac{(-\hat{i}+8\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \cdot (5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k})}{\sqrt{5^{2}+4^{2}+3^{2}}}=\frac{-5+32+3}{\sqrt{50}}=\frac{30}{5\sqrt{2}}=3\sqrt{2}$

So the projection of $3\vec{a}+\sqrt{2}\vec{b}$ onto $\vec{c}$ is $3\sqrt{2}$ which is option D.

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{u}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k},\vec{v}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k},\vec{v}.\vec{w}=2$ and $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v}$ . Then $\vec{u}.\vec{w}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{u}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k},\vec{v}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k},\vec{v}.\vec{w}=2$ and $\vec{v} \times \vec{w}=\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v}$ . Then $\vec{u}.\vec{w}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & \vec{v} \times \vec{w}=(\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v})=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k}+\lambda(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =(2\lambda+1)\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(2+\lambda)\hat{k} \\ & \end{aligned} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{v} \cdot (\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot ((2\lambda+1)\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(\lambda+2)\hat{k})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2(2\lambda+1)+\lambda-1+\lambda+2=0 \Rightarrow 6\lambda+3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \vec{w} \cdot (\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v})=\vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}+\lambda\vec{v} \cdot \vec{w}=0 \\ \\ & \vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}=-\lambda\vec{v} \cdot \vec{w} \\ \\ & \vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}=\frac{1}{2} \times 2=1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & \vec{v} \times \vec{w}=(\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v})=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k}+\lambda(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =(2\lambda+1)\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(2+\lambda)\hat{k} \\ & \end{aligned} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{v} \cdot (\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot ((2\lambda+1)\hat{i}+(\lambda-1)\hat{j}-(\lambda+2)\hat{k})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2(2\lambda+1)+\lambda-1+\lambda+2=0 \Rightarrow 6\lambda+3=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \vec{w} \cdot (\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u}+\lambda\vec{v})=\vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}+\lambda\vec{v} \cdot \vec{w}=0 \\ \\ & \vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}=-\lambda\vec{v} \cdot \vec{w} \\ \\ & \vec{u} \cdot \vec{w}=\frac{1}{2} \times 2=1 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11,\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}|$ , then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11,\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}|$ , then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|^{2}$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11 \\ \\ & \vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27 \\ \\ & \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}| \\ \\ & (\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{c}=27 \end{aligned}$ $\text{Let}\vec{c}=c_{1}\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}\hat{k}$ As $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11$ $\therefore$ $c_{1}+2c_{2}+3c_{3}=11$ ......(i) Also, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}|$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore c_{1}+c_{2}-c_{3}=-\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow c_{1}+c_{2}-c_{3}=-3......(ii) \end{aligned}$ Also, $\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27$ $\therefore$ $5c_{1}-4c_{2}+c_{3}=27$ ...........(iii) From (i), (ii) & (iii) $\vec{c}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} & |\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|^{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & +4 \end{aligned}|^{2} \\ \\ & =|14\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-8\hat{k}|^{2} \\ \\ & =14^{2}+5^{2}+8^{2}=285 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\ \\ & \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11 \\ \\ & \vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27 \\ \\ & \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}| \\ \\ & (\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{c}=27 \end{aligned}$

$\text{Let}\vec{c}=c_{1}\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}\hat{k}$

As $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=11$

$\therefore$ $c_{1}+2c_{2}+3c_{3}=11$ ......(i)

Also, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=-\sqrt{3}|\vec{b}|$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore c_{1}+c_{2}-c_{3}=-\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow c_{1}+c_{2}-c_{3}=-3......(ii) \end{aligned}$

Also, $\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})=27$

$\therefore$ $5c_{1}-4c_{2}+c_{3}=27$ ...........(iii)

From (i), (ii) & (iii)

$\vec{c}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} & |\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|^{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & +4 \end{aligned}|^{2} \\ \\ & =|14\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-8\hat{k}|^{2} \\ \\ & =14^{2}+5^{2}+8^{2}=285 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{31},4|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=2$ and $2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=3(\vec{c} \times \vec{a})$ . If the angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ , then $(\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{c}}{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}})^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html:
Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that

$|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{31},4|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=2$ and $2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=3(\vec{c} \times \vec{a})$ .

If the angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ , then $(\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{c}}{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}})^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=3(\vec{c} \times \vec{a})$ $\vec{a} \times (2\vec{b}+3\vec{c})=0$ $\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\lambda(2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}) \\ \\ & |\vec{a}|^{2}=\lambda^{2}(4|b|^{2}+9|c|^{2}+12\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}) \\ \\ & 31=31\lambda^{2} \\ \\ & \lambda= \pm 1 \\ \\ & \vec{a}= \pm (2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}) \\ \\ & \frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|}=\frac{2|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|}{2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}+3\vec{c} \cdot \vec{b}} \\ \\ & |\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot 4-(1-\frac{1}{2})^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \\ & \therefore \frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 \cdot \frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{-1} \\ \\ & (\frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|})^{2}=3 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$2(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=3(\vec{c} \times \vec{a})$

$\vec{a} \times (2\vec{b}+3\vec{c})=0$

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{a}=\lambda(2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}) \\ \\ & |\vec{a}|^{2}=\lambda^{2}(4|b|^{2}+9|c|^{2}+12\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}) \\ \\ & 31=31\lambda^{2} \\ \\ & \lambda= \pm 1 \\ \\ & \vec{a}= \pm (2\vec{b}+3\vec{c}) \\ \\ & \frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|}=\frac{2|\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|}{2\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}+3\vec{c} \cdot \vec{b}} \\ \\ & |\vec{b} \times \vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot 4-(1-\frac{1}{2})^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \\ & \therefore \frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 \cdot \frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{-1} \\ \\ & (\frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|}{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|})^{2}=3 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If the points $P$ and $Q$ are respectively the circumcenter and the orthocentre of a $△ABC$ , then $\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: 1. **Circumcenter $P$ **: The circumcenter of a triangle is equidistant from the vertices of the triangle. It is the center of the circumcircle, the circle that passes through all three vertices of the triangle. 2. **Orthocenter $Q$ **: The orthocenter of a triangle is the point of intersection of its three altitudes. An altitude of a triangle is a perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to its opposite side (or its extension). 3. **Centroid $G$ **: The centroid of a triangle is the point of intersection of its medians. A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The centroid always divides each median in a 2:1 ratio, with the larger segment being closer to the vertex. With the above definitions, it's known that the centroid divides the line segment joining the circumcenter and orthocenter in the ratio 2 : 1, meaning : $\vec{PG}=\frac{2}{3}\vec{PQ}$ $\vec{PQ}=3\vec{PG}$ The position vector of the centroid $G$ in terms of the vertices $A,B,$ and $C$ is : $\vec{G}=\frac{\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}}{3}$ Because $P$ is the circumcenter and is at the origin in this problem: $\vec{PA}=\vec{A}$ $\vec{PB}=\vec{B}$ $\vec{PC}=\vec{C}$ Substituting these into the equation for $G$ : $\vec{PG}=\frac{\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}}{3}$ Now, using the relationship between $PQ$ and $PG$ established earlier : $\vec{PQ}=3\vec{PG}=\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}$
questions.explanation_html:
1. **Circumcenter $P$ **:

The circumcenter of a triangle is equidistant from the vertices of the triangle. It is the center of the circumcircle, the circle that passes through all three vertices of the triangle.

2. **Orthocenter $Q$ **:

The orthocenter of a triangle is the point of intersection of its three altitudes. An altitude of a triangle is a perpendicular line segment drawn from a vertex to its opposite side (or its extension).

3. **Centroid $G$ **:

The centroid of a triangle is the point of intersection of its medians. A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The centroid always divides each median in a 2:1 ratio, with the larger segment being closer to the vertex.

With the above definitions, it's known that the centroid divides the line segment joining the circumcenter and orthocenter in the ratio 2 : 1, meaning :

$\vec{PG}=\frac{2}{3}\vec{PQ}$

$\vec{PQ}=3\vec{PG}$

The position vector of the centroid $G$ in terms of the vertices $A,B,$ and $C$ is :

$\vec{G}=\frac{\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}}{3}$

Because $P$ is the circumcenter and is at the origin in this problem:

$\vec{PA}=\vec{A}$

$\vec{PB}=\vec{B}$

$\vec{PC}=\vec{C}$

Substituting these into the equation for $G$ :

$\vec{PG}=\frac{\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}}{3}$

Now, using the relationship between $PQ$ and $PG$ established earlier :

$\vec{PQ}=3\vec{PG}=\vec{PA}+\vec{PB}+\vec{PC}$

Then $\underset{\lambda \in S}{\sum}(\lambda+2)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given, position vectors of the points $A,B,C$ and $D$ be $5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k},\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k},-2\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ $\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} & =(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k})=-4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+(3-2\lambda)\hat{k} \\ \\ \vec{AC} & =(-2\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+4\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =-7\hat{i}+(\lambda-5)\hat{j}+(4-2\lambda)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \text{and}\vec{AD} & =(-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+6\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =-6\hat{i}+(6-2\lambda)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ Since, points $A,B,C$ and $D$ are coplanar $\begin{aligned} & \therefore [\vec{AB}\vec{AC}\vec{AD}]=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} -4 & -3 & (3-2\lambda) \\ -7 & (\lambda-5) & (4-2\lambda) \\ -6 & 0 & 6-2\lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow -6{(-12+6\lambda)-(13\lambda-15-2\lambda^{2})} \\ \\ & +(6-2\lambda){-4\lambda+20-21}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -6(2\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+3)+(6-2\lambda)(-4\lambda-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -12\lambda^{2}+42\lambda-18+8\lambda^{2}-22\lambda-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda^{2}+20\lambda-24=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda^{2}-5\lambda+6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2,3 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore \underset{\lambda\epsilon S}{\sum}(\lambda+2)^{2}=(2+2)^{2}+(3+2)^{2}=16+25=41$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, position vectors of the points $A,B,C$ and $D$ be

$5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k},\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k},-2\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$

$\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} & =(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k})=-4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+(3-2\lambda)\hat{k} \\ \\ \vec{AC} & =(-2\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+4\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =-7\hat{i}+(\lambda-5)\hat{j}+(4-2\lambda)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \text{and}\vec{AD} & =(-\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+6\hat{k})-(5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\lambda\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =-6\hat{i}+(6-2\lambda)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

Since, points $A,B,C$ and $D$ are coplanar

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore [\vec{AB}\vec{AC}\vec{AD}]=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} -4 & -3 & (3-2\lambda) \\ -7 & (\lambda-5) & (4-2\lambda) \\ -6 & 0 & 6-2\lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow -6{(-12+6\lambda)-(13\lambda-15-2\lambda^{2})} \\ \\ & +(6-2\lambda){-4\lambda+20-21}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -6(2\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+3)+(6-2\lambda)(-4\lambda-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -12\lambda^{2}+42\lambda-18+8\lambda^{2}-22\lambda-6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -4\lambda^{2}+20\lambda-24=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda^{2}-5\lambda+6=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=2,3 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore \underset{\lambda\epsilon S}{\sum}(\lambda+2)^{2}=(2+2)^{2}+(3+2)^{2}=16+25=41$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}=6\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k},\vec{b}=\alpha\hat{i}+11\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be vectors such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ . If $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-12,\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=5$ , then $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is equal to _______________.
questions.question_html:
Let $\vec{a}=6\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k},\vec{b}=\alpha\hat{i}+11\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be vectors such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ . If

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-12,\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=5$ , then $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ is equal to _______________.
questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{c}=c_{1}\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}\hat{k}$ Now, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-12$ $\Rightarrow 6c_{1}+9c_{2}+12c_{3}=-12$ ..............(i) Also, $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=5$ $\Rightarrow c_{1}-2c_{2}+c_{3}=5$ ................(ii) $\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a} \times (\vec{c}-\vec{b})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}\text{is parallel to}(\vec{c}-\vec{b}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}=\lambda(\vec{c}-\vec{b}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k}=\lambda(c_{1}-\alpha)\hat{i}+\lambda(c_{2}-11)\hat{j}+\lambda(c_{3}+2)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$ On comparing, we get $c_{1}=\frac{6}{\lambda}+\alpha,c_{2}=\frac{9}{\lambda}+11,c_{3}=\frac{12}{\lambda}-2$ Put there values in (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} & \frac{6}{\lambda}+\alpha-\frac{18}{\lambda}-22+\frac{12}{\lambda}-2=5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=29 \end{aligned}$ From (i) and values of $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ , and $\alpha$ we have $\begin{aligned} & 6(\frac{6}{\lambda}+29)+9(\frac{9}{\lambda}+11)+12(\frac{12}{\lambda}-2)=-12 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{261}{\lambda}=-261 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}c_{1}=23,c_{2}=2,c_{3}=-14 \\ \\ & \therefore \vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=(23\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+-14\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =23+2-14=11 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{c}=c_{1}\hat{i}+c_{2}\hat{j}+c_{3}\hat{k}$

Now, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=-12$

$\Rightarrow 6c_{1}+9c_{2}+12c_{3}=-12$ ..............(i)

Also, $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})=5$

$\Rightarrow c_{1}-2c_{2}+c_{3}=5$ ................(ii)

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a} \times (\vec{c}-\vec{b})=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}\text{is parallel to}(\vec{c}-\vec{b}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{a}=\lambda(\vec{c}-\vec{b}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 6\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k}=\lambda(c_{1}-\alpha)\hat{i}+\lambda(c_{2}-11)\hat{j}+\lambda(c_{3}+2)\hat{k} \end{aligned}$

On comparing, we get

$c_{1}=\frac{6}{\lambda}+\alpha,c_{2}=\frac{9}{\lambda}+11,c_{3}=\frac{12}{\lambda}-2$

Put there values in (ii), we get

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{6}{\lambda}+\alpha-\frac{18}{\lambda}-22+\frac{12}{\lambda}-2=5 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=29 \end{aligned}$

From (i) and values of $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ , and $\alpha$ we have

$\begin{aligned} & 6(\frac{6}{\lambda}+29)+9(\frac{9}{\lambda}+11)+12(\frac{12}{\lambda}-2)=-12 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{261}{\lambda}=-261 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}c_{1}=23,c_{2}=2,c_{3}=-14 \\ \\ & \therefore \vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=(23\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+-14\hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \\ \\ & =23+2-14=11 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{14},|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{6}$ and $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=\sqrt{48}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^{2}+(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}|\vec{b}|^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 48+(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^{2}=6 \times 14 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^{2}=84-48 \\ \\ & =36 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ . Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector satisfying $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{c}$ . If $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are non-parallel, then the value of $\lambda$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ & $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=(\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{c}$ If $\vec{b}$ & $\vec{c}$ are non-parallel then $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=1$ & $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=-\lambda$ but $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=5 \Rightarrow \lambda=-5$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ & $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=(\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{c}$

If $\vec{b}$ & $\vec{c}$ are non-parallel

then $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=1$ & $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=-\lambda$

but $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=5 \Rightarrow \lambda=-5$

questions.question_text: Let a vector $\vec{a}$ has magnitude 9. Let a vector $\vec{b}$ be such that for every $(x,y) \in R \times R-{(0,0)}$ , the vector $(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b})$ is perpendicular to the vector $(6y\vec{a}-18x\vec{b})$ . Then the value of $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let a vector $\vec{a}$ has magnitude 9. Let a vector $\vec{b}$ be such that for every $(x,y) \in R \times R-{(0,0)}$ , the vector $(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b})$ is perpendicular to the vector $(6y\vec{a}-18x\vec{b})$ . Then the value of $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).(6y\vec{a}-18x\vec{b})=0$ $\Rightarrow (6xy|\vec{a}|^{2}-18xy|\vec{b}|^{2})+(6y^{2}-18x^{2})\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$ As given equation is identity Coefficient of $x^{2}=$ coefficient of $y^{2}=$ coefficient of $xy=0$ $\Rightarrow |\vec{a}|^{2}=3|\vec{b}|^{2} \Rightarrow |\vec{b}|=3\sqrt{3}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|sin\theta$ $=9.3\sqrt{3}.1=27\sqrt{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
$(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).(6y\vec{a}-18x\vec{b})=0$

$\Rightarrow (6xy|\vec{a}|^{2}-18xy|\vec{b}|^{2})+(6y^{2}-18x^{2})\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$

As given equation is identity

Coefficient of $x^{2}=$ coefficient of $y^{2}=$ coefficient of $xy=0$

$\Rightarrow |\vec{a}|^{2}=3|\vec{b}|^{2} \Rightarrow |\vec{b}|=3\sqrt{3}$

and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and let $\vec{b}$ be a vector such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=3$ . Then the projection of $\vec{b}$ on the vector $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ is :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and let $\vec{b}$ be a vector such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=3$ . Then the projection of $\vec{b}$ on the vector $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=3$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{a}.\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}.|\vec{b}|^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 5+9=6|\vec{b}|^{2}$ $\Rightarrow |b|^{2}=\frac{7}{3}$ $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|=\sqrt{|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}-2\vec{a}.\vec{b}}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}$ projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}-\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{b}.(\vec{a}-\vec{b})}{|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|}$ $=\frac{\vec{b}.\vec{a}-|\vec{b}|^{2}}{|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|}=\frac{3-\frac{7}{3}}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}}$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-\hat{k}$

$\vec{a}.\vec{b}=3$

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{a}.\vec{b}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}.|\vec{b}|^{2}$

$\Rightarrow 5+9=6|\vec{b}|^{2}$

$\Rightarrow |b|^{2}=\frac{7}{3}$

$|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|=\sqrt{|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}-2\vec{a}.\vec{b}}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}$

projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}-\vec{b}=\frac{\vec{b}.(\vec{a}-\vec{b})}{|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|}$

$=\frac{\vec{b}.\vec{a}-|\vec{b}|^{2}}{|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|}=\frac{3-\frac{7}{3}}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}}$

$=\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}}$

If the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{10}{3}$ and $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ , then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ , $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\beta\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ where $\alpha,\beta \in R$ , be three vectors. If the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{10}{3}$ and $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ , then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\beta\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ $\vec{c}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{c}}{|\vec{b}|}=\frac{10}{3}$ $\frac{\alpha+6+2}{\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+(-2)^{2}}}=\frac{\alpha+8}{3}=\frac{10}{3}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 2 $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -\beta & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \end{aligned}|=(2\beta-8)\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+(6+\beta)\hat{k}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ $2\beta-8=-6$ & $6+\beta=7$ $\therefore$ $\beta$ = 1 $\alpha+\beta=2+1=3$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\beta\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$

$\vec{c}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$ is

$\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{c}}{|\vec{b}|}=\frac{10}{3}$

$\frac{\alpha+6+2}{\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+(-2)^{2}}}=\frac{\alpha+8}{3}=\frac{10}{3}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 2

$\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$

$|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -\beta & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \end{aligned}|=(2\beta-8)\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+(6+\beta)\hat{k}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$

$2\beta-8=-6$ & $6+\beta=7$

$\therefore$ $\beta$ = 1

$\alpha+\beta=2+1=3$
