questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ be two vectors. If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=0$ , then $\vec{c}.\vec{b}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $|\vec{a}|$ = $\sqrt{6}$ , $|\vec{b}|$ = $\sqrt{3}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}$ = 4 Given $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ $(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ - $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{b} \times (\vec{c}-\vec{a})$ = 0 $\therefore$ $\vec{b}\parallel(\vec{c}-\vec{a})$ $\Rightarrow$ $(\vec{c}-\vec{a})=\lambda\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}=\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=\vec{a}.\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{a}.\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ 0 = $|\vec{a}|^{2}+\lambda(\vec{a}.\vec{b})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{-|\vec{a}|^{2}}{\vec{a}.\vec{b}}$ = $\frac{-6}{4}=-\frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{c}$ = $\vec{a}-\frac{3}{2}\vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}$ = ( $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ ) - $\frac{3}{2}$ ( $\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ ) $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ $\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{b}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ ( $\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ ) $\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{b}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\vec{b}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$|\vec{a}|$ = $\sqrt{6}$ , $|\vec{b}|$ = $\sqrt{3}$

and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}$ = 4

Given $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ - $(\vec{b} \times \vec{a})$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{b} \times (\vec{c}-\vec{a})$ = 0

$\therefore$ $\vec{b}\parallel(\vec{c}-\vec{a})$

$\Rightarrow$ $(\vec{c}-\vec{a})=\lambda\vec{b}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}=\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{b}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=\vec{a}.\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{a}.\vec{b}$

$\Rightarrow$ 0 = $|\vec{a}|^{2}+\lambda(\vec{a}.\vec{b})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{-|\vec{a}|^{2}}{\vec{a}.\vec{b}}$ = $\frac{-6}{4}=-\frac{3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{c}$ = $\vec{a}-\frac{3}{2}\vec{b}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}$ = ( $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ ) - $\frac{3}{2}$ ( $\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ )

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{c}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$

$\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{b}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ ( $\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ )

$\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{b}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}$

questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{a}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ Now $\hat{i} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{i})=(\hat{i}.\hat{i})\vec{a}-(\hat{i}.\vec{a})\hat{i}$ = $y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ Similarly $\hat{j} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{j})=x\hat{i}+z\hat{k}$ $\hat{k} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{k})=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}$ Now $|y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}|^{2}+|x\hat{i}+z\hat{k}|^{2}+|x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}|^{2}$ = $2(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2})$ Given $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ x = 2, y = 1, z = 2 = 2(4 + 1 + 4) = 18
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{a}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

Now $\hat{i} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{i})=(\hat{i}.\hat{i})\vec{a}-(\hat{i}.\vec{a})\hat{i}$

= $y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

Similarly $\hat{j} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{j})=x\hat{i}+z\hat{k}$

$\hat{k} \times (\vec{a} \times \hat{k})=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}$

Now $|y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}|^{2}+|x\hat{i}+z\hat{k}|^{2}+|x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}|^{2}$

= $2(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2})$

Given $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ x = 2, y = 1, z = 2

= 2(4 + 1 + 4) = 18

If the vectors, $\vec{p}=(a+1)\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+a\hat{k}$ , $\vec{q}=a\hat{i}+(a+1)\hat{j}+a\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}=a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+(a+1)\hat{k}(a \in R)$ are coplanar
and $3(\vec{p}.\vec{q})^{2}-\lambda|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=0$ , then the value of $\lambda$ is ______.
questions.question_html:
If the vectors, $\vec{p}=(a+1)\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+a\hat{k}$ ,

$\vec{q}=a\hat{i}+(a+1)\hat{j}+a\hat{k}$ and

$\vec{r}=a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+(a+1)\hat{k}(a \in R)$

are coplanar and $3(\vec{p}.\vec{q})^{2}-\lambda|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=0$ , then the value of $\lambda$ is ______.
questions.explanation_text: $\because$ $\vec{p}$ , $\vec{q}$ , $\vec{r}$ are coplanar $\therefore$ $[\begin{aligned} \vec{p} & \vec{q} & \vec{r} \end{aligned}]$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $|\begin{aligned} a+1 & a & a \\ a & a+1 & a \\ a & a & a+1 \end{aligned}|$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ (a + 1) + a + a = 0 $\Rightarrow$ a = $-\frac{1}{3}$ $\vec{p}.\vec{q}$ = $\frac{1}{9}(-2-2+1)$ = $-\frac{1}{3}$ $\vec{r} \times \vec{q}$ = $\frac{1}{9}|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{aligned}|$ = $\frac{1}{9}(3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ = $\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=\frac{1}{3}$ Also $3(\vec{p}.\vec{q})^{2}-\lambda|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $3(\frac{1}{9})-\lambda(\frac{1}{3})$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = 1
questions.explanation_html:
$\because$ $\vec{p}$ , $\vec{q}$ , $\vec{r}$ are coplanar

$\therefore$ $[\begin{aligned} \vec{p} & \vec{q} & \vec{r} \end{aligned}]$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $|\begin{aligned} a+1 & a & a \\ a & a+1 & a \\ a & a & a+1 \end{aligned}|$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ (a + 1) + a + a = 0

$\Rightarrow$ a = $-\frac{1}{3}$

$\vec{p}.\vec{q}$ = $\frac{1}{9}(-2-2+1)$ = $-\frac{1}{3}$

$\vec{r} \times \vec{q}$ = $\frac{1}{9}|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{aligned}|$

= $\frac{1}{9}(3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$

= $\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=\frac{1}{3}$

Also $3(\vec{p}.\vec{q})^{2}-\lambda|\vec{r} \times \vec{q}|^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $3(\frac{1}{9})-\lambda(\frac{1}{3})$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = 1

Given $\vec{\alpha}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ $\vec{\beta}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ is parallel to $\vec{\alpha}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $\lambda$ $\vec{\alpha}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $3\lambda\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}$ $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ is perpendicular
to $\vec{\alpha}$ $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ . $\vec{\alpha}$ = 0 Let $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ ( $x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ ).( $3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ ) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 3x + y = 0 $\Rightarrow$ y = -3x $\therefore$ $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $x\hat{i}-3x\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ Given $\vec{\beta}=\vec{\beta}_{1}-\vec{\beta_{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ ) = ( $3\lambda\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}$ ) - ( $x\hat{i}-3x\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ ) = $(3\lambda-x)\hat{i}+(\lambda+3x)\hat{j}-z\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ 3 $\lambda$ - x = 2 ...(1) $\lambda$ + 3x = -1.....(2) z = -3 Solving (1) and (2), we get $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ and x = $-\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $\frac{3}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{j}$ and $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{3}{2}\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ $\vec{\beta}_{1} \times \vec{\beta}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} & -3 \end{aligned}|$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ ( $-3\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ )

Given $\vec{\alpha}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$

$\vec{\beta}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$\vec{\beta}_{1}$ is parallel to $\vec{\alpha}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $\lambda$ $\vec{\alpha}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $3\lambda\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}$

$\vec{\beta_{2}}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{\alpha}$

$\vec{\beta_{2}}$ . $\vec{\alpha}$ = 0

Let $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ ( $x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ ).( $3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ ) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ 3x + y = 0

$\Rightarrow$ y = -3x

$\therefore$ $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $x\hat{i}-3x\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$

Given $\vec{\beta}=\vec{\beta}_{1}-\vec{\beta_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ ) = ( $3\lambda\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}$ ) - ( $x\hat{i}-3x\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ )

= $(3\lambda-x)\hat{i}+(\lambda+3x)\hat{j}-z\hat{k}$

$\therefore$ 3 $\lambda$ - x = 2 ...(1)

$\lambda$ + 3x = -1.....(2)

z = -3

Solving (1) and (2), we get

$\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ and x = $-\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ = $\frac{3}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{j}$

and $\vec{\beta_{2}}$ = $-\frac{1}{2}\hat{i}+\frac{3}{2}\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$

$\vec{\beta}_{1} \times \vec{\beta}_{2}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} & -3 \end{aligned}|$

= $\frac{1}{2}$ ( $-3\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ )

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=3\overset{\wedge}{i}+2\overset{\wedge}{j}+x\overset{\wedge}{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\overset{\wedge}{i}-\overset{\wedge}{j}+\overset{\wedge}{k}$ , for some real x. Then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ = r is possible if :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 2 & x \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ = (2 + x) $\hat{i}$ + (3 - x) $\hat{j}$ - 5 $\hat{k}$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ = r = $\sqrt{(2+x)^{2}+(x-3)^{2}+(-5)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ r = $\sqrt{4+4x+x^{2}+x^{2}+9-6x+25}$ = $\sqrt{2x^{2}-2x+38}$ = $\sqrt{2(x^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4})+38-\frac{1}{2}}$ = $\sqrt{2(x-\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{75}{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ r $\ge$ $\sqrt{\frac{75}{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $r \ge 5\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:

= (2 + x) $\hat{i}$ + (3 - x) $\hat{j}$ - 5 $\hat{k}$

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ = r

= $\sqrt{(2+x)^{2}+(x-3)^{2}+(-5)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ r = $\sqrt{4+4x+x^{2}+x^{2}+9-6x+25}$

= $\sqrt{2(x-\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{75}{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ r $\ge$ $\sqrt{\frac{75}{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $r \ge 5\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$

questions.question_html: Let   $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k},$   $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$  and  $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+(\lambda^{2}-1)\hat{k}$  be coplanar vectors. Then the non-zero vector $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]=0$ $\Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & \lambda & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & \lambda^{2}-1 \end{aligned}|=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda^{3}-2\lambda^{2}-9\lambda+18=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda^{2}(\lambda-2)-9(\lambda-2)=0$ $\Rightarrow (\lambda-3)(\lambda+3)(\lambda-2)=0$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=2,3,-3$ So, $\lambda$ = 2 (as $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $\vec{c}$ for $\lambda$ = $\pm$ 3) Hence $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \end{aligned}|$ $=-10\hat{i}+5\hat{j}$
questions.explanation_html:
$[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]=0$

$\Rightarrow |\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & \lambda & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & \lambda^{2}-1 \end{aligned}|=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda^{3}-2\lambda^{2}-9\lambda+18=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda^{2}(\lambda-2)-9(\lambda-2)=0$

$\Rightarrow (\lambda-3)(\lambda+3)(\lambda-2)=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=2,3,-3$

So,    $\lambda$ = 2 (as    $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $\vec{c}$ for $\lambda$ = $\pm$ 3)

Hence    $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \end{aligned}|$

$=-10\hat{i}+5\hat{j}$

Let $\vec{a}$ = $\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ , $\vec{b}$ = $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$

be a vector such that $\vec{a}$ × $\vec{c}$ + $\vec{b}$ = $\vec{0}$

and $\vec{a}$ . $\vec{c}$ = 4, then | $\vec{c}$ |2 is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given that, $\vec{a} \times \vec{c}+\vec{b}=\vec{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})\vec{a}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})\vec{c}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$ given that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=4$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=|\vec{a}|^{2}=(\sqrt{2})^{2}=2$ $\Rightarrow$ $4\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=0$ Now $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ $=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $2\vec{c}=4(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ $=4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $=3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{c}=\frac{3}{2}\hat{i}-\frac{5}{2}\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{25}{4}+1}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{38}{4}}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{19}{2}}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{19}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given that,

$\vec{a} \times \vec{c}+\vec{b}=\vec{0}$

$\Rightarrow$    $\vec{a} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$

$\Rightarrow$    $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c})\vec{a}-(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a})\vec{c}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\vec{0}$

given that

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}=4$

and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}=|\vec{a}|^{2}=(\sqrt{2})^{2}=2$

$\Rightarrow$    $4\vec{a}-2\vec{c}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=0$

Now   $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$

$=|\begin{aligned} i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

$\therefore$    $2\vec{c}=4(\hat{i}-\hat{j})+(-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$

$=4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$=3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\therefore$    $\vec{c}=\frac{3}{2}\hat{i}-\frac{5}{2}\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$\therefore$    $|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{25}{4}+1}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{38}{4}}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{19}{2}}$

$\therefore$    $|\vec{c}|^{2}=\frac{19}{2}$

A unit vector $\vec{a}$ makes angles $\pi$ /3 with $\hat{i}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha$ = $\pi$ /3 and $\pi$ / 4

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{u}$ be a vector coplanar with the vectors $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ . If $\vec{u}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{u}.\vec{b}=24$ , then $|\vec{u}|^{2}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: You should know that, when $\vec{u}$ is coplanar with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ then we can write $\vec{u}=x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}$ Here, $\vec{u}$ is perpendicular with $\vec{a}$ then, $\vec{u}.\vec{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow (x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow x.\vec{a}.\vec{a}+y.\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$ $\Rightarrow x.|\vec{a}|^{2}+y\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$ [ As $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{14}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}).(\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ $=(2.0+3.1+(-1).1)$ $=2$ ] $\Rightarrow x.(14)+y.2=0$ $\Rightarrow 7x+y=0........(1)$ Given, $\vec{u}.\vec{b}=24$ $\Rightarrow (x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{b}=24$ $\Rightarrow x(\vec{a}.\vec{b})+y|\vec{b}|^{2}=24$ $\Rightarrow x.2+y.(\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}})^{2}=24$ $\Rightarrow 2x+2y=24$ $\Rightarrow x+y=12.......(2)$ By solvig (1) and (2) we get, x = - 2 and y = 14 Now, $|\vec{u}|^{2}=\vec{u}.\vec{u}$ $=(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{u}$ $=x\vec{a}.\vec{u}+y\vec{b}.\vec{u}$ $=x\vec{a}.\vec{u}+y\vec{b}.\vec{u}$ $=0+14 \times 24$ [as $\vec{a}.\vec{u}=0$ and $\vec{u}.\vec{b}=24]$ $=$ 336
questions.explanation_html:
You should know that, when $\vec{u}$ is coplanar with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ then we can write $\vec{u}=x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}$

Here, $\vec{u}$ is perpendicular with $\vec{a}$ then,

$\vec{u}.\vec{a}=0$

$\Rightarrow (x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{a}=0$

$\Rightarrow x.\vec{a}.\vec{a}+y.\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$

$\Rightarrow x.|\vec{a}|^{2}+y\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0$

[ As $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{14}$

and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}).(\hat{j}+\hat{k})$

$=(2.0+3.1+(-1).1)$

$=2$ ]

$\Rightarrow x.(14)+y.2=0$

$\Rightarrow 7x+y=0........(1)$

Given, $\vec{u}.\vec{b}=24$

$\Rightarrow (x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{b}=24$

$\Rightarrow x(\vec{a}.\vec{b})+y|\vec{b}|^{2}=24$

$\Rightarrow x.2+y.(\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}})^{2}=24$

$\Rightarrow 2x+2y=24$

$\Rightarrow x+y=12.......(2)$

By solvig (1) and (2) we get,

x = - 2 and y = 14

Now, $|\vec{u}|^{2}=\vec{u}.\vec{u}$

$=(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}).\vec{u}$

$=x\vec{a}.\vec{u}+y\vec{b}.\vec{u}$

$=x\vec{a}.\vec{u}+y\vec{b}.\vec{u}$

$=0+14 \times 24$ [as $\vec{a}.\vec{u}=0$ and $\vec{u}.\vec{b}=24]$

$=$ 336

questions.question_text: If the position vectors of the vertices A, B and C of a $\Delta$ ABC are respectively $4\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+8\hat{k},$ $2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},$ and $2\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+7\hat{k},$ then the position vectors of the point, where the bisector of $\angle$ A meets BC is :
questions.question_html: If the position vectors of the vertices A, B and C of a $\Delta$ ABC are respectively $4\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+8\hat{k},$     $2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k},$ and $2\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+7\hat{k},$ then the position vectors of the point, where the bisector of $\angle$ A meets BC is :
questions.explanation_text: Suppose angular bisector of A meets BC at D(x, , z) Using angular bisector theorem, $\frac{AB}{AC}$ = $\frac{BD}{DC}$ $\frac{BD}{DC}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{(4-2)^{2}+(7-3)^{2}+(8-4)^{2}}}{\sqrt{(4-2)^{2}+(7-5)^{2}+(8-7)^{2}}}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{2^{2}+4^{2}+4^{2}}}{\sqrt{2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}}$ = $\frac{6}{3}$ = 2 So, D(x, y, z) $\equiv$ $(\frac{(2)(2)+(1)(2)}{2+1},\frac{(2)(5)+(1)(3)}{2+1}$ , $\frac{(2)(7)+(1)(4)}{2+1})$ D(x, y, z) $\equiv$ $(\frac{6}{3},\frac{13}{3},\frac{18}{3})$ Therefore, position vector of point p = $\frac{1}{3}$ (6i + 13j + 18k)
questions.explanation_html:
Suppose angular bisector of A meets BC at D(x, , z)

Using angular bisector theorem,

$\frac{AB}{AC}$ = $\frac{BD}{DC}$

$\frac{BD}{DC}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{(4-2)^{2}+(7-3)^{2}+(8-4)^{2}}}{\sqrt{(4-2)^{2}+(7-5)^{2}+(8-7)^{2}}}$

= $\frac{\sqrt{2^{2}+4^{2}+4^{2}}}{\sqrt{2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}}$ = $\frac{6}{3}$ = 2



So, D(x, y, z) $\equiv$ $(\frac{(2)(2)+(1)(2)}{2+1},\frac{(2)(5)+(1)(3)}{2+1}$ , $\frac{(2)(7)+(1)(4)}{2+1})$

D(x, y, z) $\equiv$ $(\frac{6}{3},\frac{13}{3},\frac{18}{3})$

Therefore, position vector of point p = $\frac{1}{3}$ (6i + 13j + 18k)

questions.question_html: If $\vec{a},\vec{b},$ and $\vec{C}$ are unit vectors such that $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+2\vec{c}=\vec{0},$ then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+2\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}+2\vec{c}=-2\vec{b}$ Squaring both sides, $|\vec{a}|^{2}+4\vec{a}.\vec{c}+4|\vec{c}|^{2}=4|\vec{b}|^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 1 + $4\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ + 4 = 4   [as $|\vec{a}|^{2}$ = $|\vec{b}|^{2}$ = $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ = 1] $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=-\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|cos\theta=-\frac{1}{4}$ $\therefore$ $cos\theta$ = $-\frac{1}{4}$ $\therefore$ $sin^{2}\theta$ = 1 - $cos^{2}\theta$ = 1 - $\frac{1}{16}$ = $\frac{15}{16}$ $\therefore$ sin $\theta$ = $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|sin\theta$ = 1 . 1 . $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\vec{a}+2\vec{b}+2\vec{c}=\vec{0}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}+2\vec{c}=-2\vec{b}$

Squaring both sides,

$|\vec{a}|^{2}+4\vec{a}.\vec{c}+4|\vec{c}|^{2}=4|\vec{b}|^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ 1 + $4\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ + 4 = 4   [as $|\vec{a}|^{2}$ = $|\vec{b}|^{2}$ = $|\vec{c}|^{2}$ = 1]

$\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=-\frac{1}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|cos\theta=-\frac{1}{4}$

$\therefore$ $cos\theta$ = $-\frac{1}{4}$

$\therefore$ $sin^{2}\theta$ = 1 - $cos^{2}\theta$

= 1 - $\frac{1}{16}$

= $\frac{15}{16}$

$\therefore$ sin $\theta$ = $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$

$\therefore$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{c}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|sin\theta$

= 1 . 1 . $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$

= $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$

questions.question_html: The area (in sq. units) of the parallelogram whose diagonals are along the vectors $8\hat{i}-6\hat{j}$ and $3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-12\hat{k},$ is :
questions.explanation_text: When diagonal $\vec{d_{1}}$ and $\vec{d_{2}}$ are given of a parallelogram then the area of parallelogram = $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{d_{1}} \times \vec{d_{2}}|$ Given, $\vec{d_{1}}$ = 8 $\hat{i}$ $-$ 6 $\hat{j}$ + 0 $\hat{k}$ and $\vec{d_{2}}$ = 3 $\hat{i}$ + 4 $\hat{j}$ $-$ 12 $\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{d_{1}}$ $\times$ $\vec{d_{2}}$ = $|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 8 & -6 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & -12 \end{aligned}|$ = 72 $\hat{i}$ $-$ ( $-$ 96) $\hat{j}$ + 50 $\hat{k}$ = 72 $\hat{i}$ + 96 $\hat{j}$ + 50 $\hat{k}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{d_{1}} \times \vec{d_{2}}|$ = $\sqrt{72^{2}+96^{2}+50^{2}}$ = $\sqrt{16900}$ = 130 $\therefore$ Area of parallelogram = $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{d_{1}} \times \vec{d_{2}}|$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ 130 = 65

and    $\vec{d_{2}}$ = 3 $\hat{i}$ + 4 $\hat{j}$ $-$ 12 $\hat{k}$

= 130

Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|=3$ , $|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}|=3$ and the angle between $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is $30^{\circ}$ . Then $\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ .

Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|=3$ ,

$|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}|=3$ and the angle between $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is $30^{\circ}$ .

Then $\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given: $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ $\Rightarrow$ $|\vec{a}|=3$ $\therefore$ $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}=3$ We have $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}||\vec{c}|sin30^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow$ $|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}|=3|\vec{c}|.\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $3=3|\vec{c}|.\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $|\vec{c}|=2$ Now $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|=3$ On squaring, we get $\Rightarrow$ $c^{2}+a^{2}-2-\vec{c}.\vec{a}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $4+9-2-\vec{a}.\vec{c}=9$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=2$ [ $\because$ $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ ]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

$\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k},\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$

$\Rightarrow$    $|\vec{a}|=3$

$\therefore$    $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|=\sqrt{2^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}=3$

We have $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}||\vec{c}|sin30^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow$    $|(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}|=3|\vec{c}|.\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$    $3=3|\vec{c}|.\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$    $|\vec{c}|=2$

Now   $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|=3$

On squaring, we get

$\Rightarrow$    $c^{2}+a^{2}-2-\vec{c}.\vec{a}=9$

$\Rightarrow$    $4+9-2-\vec{a}.\vec{c}=9$

$\Rightarrow$    $\vec{a}.\vec{c}=2$     [ $\because$    $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=\vec{a}.\vec{c}$ ]

questions.question_html: Let ABC be a triangle whose circumcentre is at P. If the position vectors of A, B, C and P are $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ and $\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{4}$ respectively, then the position vector of the orthocentre of this triangle, is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, Position vector of circumcentre, $\vec{C}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{4}$ We know, position vector of centroid, $\vec{G}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{3}$ Now, let $\vec{R}$ be the orthocentre of the triangle. We know, $\vec{G}$ $=\frac{2\vec{C}+\vec{R}}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ 3 $\vec{G}$ $=2\vec{C}+\vec{R}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec{R}=3\vec{G}-2\vec{C}$ = $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})-2(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{4})$ = $\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

Position vector of circumcentre, $\vec{C}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{4}$

We know, position vector of centroid, $\vec{G}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{3}$

Now, let $\vec{R}$ be the orthocentre of the triangle.

We know, $\vec{G}$ $=\frac{2\vec{C}+\vec{R}}{3}$

$\Rightarrow$    3 $\vec{G}$ $=2\vec{C}+\vec{R}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\vec{R}=3\vec{G}-2\vec{C}$

=    $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})-2(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{4})$

=    $\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}}{2}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three non-zero vectors such that no two of them are collinear and $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}.$ If $\theta$ is the angle between vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , then a value of sin $\theta$ is :
questions.question_html:
Let $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three non-zero vectors such that no two of them are collinear and

$(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}.$ If $\theta$ is the angle between vectors $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ , then a value of sin $\theta$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$ $\Rightarrow -\vec{c} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$ $\Rightarrow -(\vec{c}.\vec{b})\vec{a}+(\vec{c}.\vec{a})\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$ $\Rightarrow -|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|cos\theta\vec{a}+(\vec{c}.\vec{a})\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are non collinear, the above equation is possible only when $-cos\theta=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow cos\theta=-\frac{1}{3}$ $\Rightarrow sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3};\theta \in II$ quad
questions.explanation_html:
$(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$

$\Rightarrow -\vec{c} \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$

$\Rightarrow -(\vec{c}.\vec{b})\vec{a}+(\vec{c}.\vec{a})\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$

$\Rightarrow -|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|cos\theta\vec{a}+(\vec{c}.\vec{a})\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\vec{a}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are non collinear, the above equation is possible only when

$-cos\theta=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\vec{c}.\vec{a}=0$

$\Rightarrow cos\theta=-\frac{1}{3}$

$\Rightarrow sin\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3};\theta \in II$ quad

questions.question_text: If $[\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\vec{b} \times \vec{c}\vec{c} \times \vec{a}]=\lambda[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$ then $\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If $[\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\vec{b} \times \vec{c}\vec{c} \times \vec{a}]=\lambda[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$ then $\lambda$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $L.H.S$ $=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \times (\vec{c} \times \vec{a})]$ $=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{a})]\vec{c}-(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{c})\vec{a}]$ $=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[[\vec{b}\vec{c}\vec{a}]\vec{c}]$ $[$ As $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{c}=0$ $]$ $=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}].(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}.\vec{c})=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$ $[\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\vec{b} \times \vec{c}\vec{c} \times \vec{a}]=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$ So $\lambda=1$
questions.explanation_html:
$L.H.S$ $=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \times (\vec{c} \times \vec{a})]$

$=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{a})]\vec{c}-(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{c})\vec{a}]$

$=(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}).[[\vec{b}\vec{c}\vec{a}]\vec{c}]$ $[$ As $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}.\vec{c}=0$ $]$

$=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}].(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}.\vec{c})=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$

$[\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\vec{b} \times \vec{c}\vec{c} \times \vec{a}]=[\vec{a}\vec{b}\vec{c}]^{2}$

So $\lambda=1$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two unit vectors. If the vectors $\vec{c}=\hat{a}+2\hat{b}$ and $\vec{d}=5\hat{a}-4\hat{b}$ are perpendicular to each other, then the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $\vec{c}=\hat{a}+2\hat{b}$ and $\vec{d}=5\hat{a}-4\hat{b}$ Since $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{d}$ are perpendicular to each other $\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{d}=0 \Rightarrow (\hat{a}+2\hat{b}).(5\hat{a}-4\hat{b})=0$ $\Rightarrow 5+6\hat{a}.\hat{b}-8=0$ (as $\hat{a}.\hat{a}=1$ ) $\Rightarrow \hat{a}.\hat{b}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\vec{c}=\hat{a}+2\hat{b}$ and $\vec{d}=5\hat{a}-4\hat{b}$

Since $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{d}$ are perpendicular to each other

$\therefore$ $\vec{c}.\vec{d}=0 \Rightarrow (\hat{a}+2\hat{b}).(5\hat{a}-4\hat{b})=0$

$\Rightarrow 5+6\hat{a}.\hat{b}-8=0$ (as $\hat{a}.\hat{a}=1$ )

$\Rightarrow \hat{a}.\hat{b}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.question_text: Let $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , $\vec{c}$ be three non-zero vectors which are pairwise non-collinear. If $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ , then $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ is :
questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , $\vec{c}$ be three non-zero vectors which are pairwise non-collinear. If $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ , then $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: We are given that $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ . This means we can write: $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{c}...(i)$ $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}=\mu\vec{a}...(ii)$ for some scalars $\lambda$ and $\mu$ . We are trying to find $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ in terms of $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ . We can also express this as : $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=(\lambda+6)\vec{c}...(iii)$ by adding $6\vec{c}$ to both sides of equation (i). Now, from equation (ii), multiplying by 3 gives us : $3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=3\mu\vec{a}...(iv)$ Adding $\vec{a}$ to both sides of equation (iv) gives : $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=(1+3\mu)\vec{a}...(v)$ Now, we have two expressions for $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ , one in terms of $\vec{c}$ (from equation iii) and one in terms of $\vec{a}$ (from equation v). Setting these equal to each other gives : $(\lambda+6)\vec{c}=(1+3\mu)\vec{a}...(vi)$ Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ are not collinear, this equation can only hold if the coefficients on both sides are zero, hence : $\lambda+6=0$ and $1+3\mu=0$ This gives $\lambda=-6$ and $\mu=-\frac{1}{3}$ . Finally, substituting $\lambda=-6$ into equation (iii) gives : $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=0$ So, $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ . Therefore, the correct answer is Option D : $\vec{0}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
We are given that $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{c}$ , and $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ . This means we can write:

  1. $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}=\lambda\vec{c}...(i)$
  2. $\vec{b}+2\vec{c}=\mu\vec{a}...(ii)$

for some scalars $\lambda$ and $\mu$ .

We are trying to find $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ in terms of $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ . We can also express this as :

$\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=(\lambda+6)\vec{c}...(iii)$

by adding $6\vec{c}$ to both sides of equation (i).

Now, from equation (ii), multiplying by 3 gives us :

$3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=3\mu\vec{a}...(iv)$

Adding $\vec{a}$ to both sides of equation (iv) gives :

$\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=(1+3\mu)\vec{a}...(v)$

Now, we have two expressions for $\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}$ , one in terms of $\vec{c}$ (from equation iii) and one in terms of $\vec{a}$ (from equation v). Setting these equal to each other gives :

$(\lambda+6)\vec{c}=(1+3\mu)\vec{a}...(vi)$

Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ are not collinear, this equation can only hold if the coefficients on both sides are zero, hence :

$\lambda+6=0$ and $1+3\mu=0$

This gives $\lambda=-6$ and $\mu=-\frac{1}{3}$ .

Finally, substituting $\lambda=-6$ into equation (iii) gives :

$\vec{a}+3\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=0$

So, $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+6\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ .

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D : $\vec{0}$ .

questions.question_text: The vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are not perpendicular and $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{d}$ are two vectors satisfying $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{d}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{d}=0.$ Then the vector $\vec{d}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: The vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are not perpendicular and $\vec{c}$ and $\vec{d}$ are two vectors satisfying $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{d}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{d}=0.$ Then the vector $\vec{d}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{a}.\vec{b} \ne 0,\vec{a}.\vec{d}=0$ Now, $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{d}$ $\Rightarrow \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{d})$ $\Rightarrow (\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}=(\vec{a}.\vec{d})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{d}$ $\Rightarrow (\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{d}=-(\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}+(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}$ $\vec{d}=\vec{c}-(\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{c}}{\vec{a}.\vec{b}})\vec{b}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{a}.\vec{b} \ne 0,\vec{a}.\vec{d}=0$

Now, $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{d}$

$\Rightarrow \vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})=\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{d})$

$\Rightarrow (\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}=(\vec{a}.\vec{d})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{d}$

$\Rightarrow (\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{d}=-(\vec{a}.\vec{c})\vec{b}+(\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{c}$

$\vec{d}=\vec{c}-(\frac{\vec{a}.\vec{c}}{\vec{a}.\vec{b}})\vec{b}$

questions.question_html:
If $\vec{a}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3\hat{i}+\hat{k})$ and $\vec{b}=\frac{1}{7}(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}),$ then the value

of $(2\vec{a}-\vec{b})[(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a}+2\vec{b})]$ is :
questions.explanation_text: We have $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0,\vec{a}.\vec{a}=1,\vec{b}.\vec{b}=1$ $(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a}+2\vec{b})]$ $=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[{\vec{a}.(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})}\vec{b}-{\vec{b}.(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})\vec{a}}]$ $=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[(\vec{a}.\vec{a}+2\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b}+2\vec{b}.\vec{b})\vec{a}]$ $=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[\vec{b}-2\vec{a}]$ $=4\vec{a}.\vec{b}-\vec{b}.\vec{b}-4\vec{a}.\vec{a}$ $=-5$
questions.explanation_html:
We have $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=0,\vec{a}.\vec{a}=1,\vec{b}.\vec{b}=1$

$(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a}+2\vec{b})]$

$=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[{\vec{a}.(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})}\vec{b}-{\vec{b}.(\vec{a}+2\vec{b})\vec{a}}]$

$=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[(\vec{a}.\vec{a}+2\vec{a}.\vec{b})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}.\vec{b}+2\vec{b}.\vec{b})\vec{a}]$

$=(2\vec{a}-\vec{b}).[\vec{b}-2\vec{a}]$

$=4\vec{a}.\vec{b}-\vec{b}.\vec{b}-4\vec{a}.\vec{a}$

$=-5$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}.$ Then the vector $\vec{b}$ satisfying $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}+\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=3$ :
questions.explanation_text: $\vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ $\Rightarrow \vec{b}.\vec{c}=\vec{b}.(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \Rightarrow \vec{b}.\vec{c}=0$ $\Rightarrow (b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}).(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k})=0,$ where $\vec{b}=b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}$ $b_{1}-b_{2}-b_{3}=0....(i)$ and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=3$ $\Rightarrow (\hat{j}-\hat{k}).(b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k})=3$ $\Rightarrow b_{2}-b_{3}=3$ From equation $(i)$ $b_{1}=b_{2}+b_{3}=(3+b_{3})+b_{3}=3+2b_{3}$ $\vec{b}=(3+2b_{3})\hat{i}+(3+b_{3})\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}$ From the option given, it is clear that $b_{3}$ equal to either $2$ or $-2.$ $b_{3}=2$ then $\vec{b}=7\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ which is not possible If $b_{3}=-2,$ then $\vec{b}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\vec{c}=\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$

$\Rightarrow \vec{b}.\vec{c}=\vec{b}.(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}) \Rightarrow \vec{b}.\vec{c}=0$

$\Rightarrow (b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}).(\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k})=0,$

where $\vec{b}=b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}$

$b_{1}-b_{2}-b_{3}=0....(i)$

and $\vec{a}.\vec{b}=3$

$\Rightarrow (\hat{j}-\hat{k}).(b_{1}\hat{i}+b_{2}\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k})=3$

$\Rightarrow b_{2}-b_{3}=3$

From equation $(i)$

$b_{1}=b_{2}+b_{3}=(3+b_{3})+b_{3}=3+2b_{3}$

$\vec{b}=(3+2b_{3})\hat{i}+(3+b_{3})\hat{j}+b_{3}\hat{k}$

From the option given, it is clear that $b_{3}$ equal to either $2$ or $-2.$

$b_{3}=2$

then $\vec{b}=7\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ which is not possible

If $b_{3}=-2,$ then $\vec{b}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

questions.explanation_text: $[3\vec{u}p\vec{v}p\vec{\omega}]-[p\vec{v}\vec{\omega}q\vec{u}]-[2\vec{\omega}q\vec{v}q\vec{u}]=0$ $\Rightarrow (3p^{2}-pq+2q^{2})[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{\omega}]=0$ $\Rightarrow 3p^{2}-pq+2q^{2}=0$ $($ As $[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{\omega}] \ne 0$ $)$ $\Rightarrow 2p^{2}+p^{2}-pq+\frac{q^{2}}{4}+\frac{7q^{2}}{4}=0$ $\Rightarrow 2p^{2}+(p-\frac{q}{2})^{2}+\frac{7}{4}q^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow p=0,q=0,p=\frac{q}{2}$ $\Rightarrow p=0,q=0$ $\therefore$ Exactly one value of $(p,q)$
questions.explanation_html:
$[3\vec{u}p\vec{v}p\vec{\omega}]-[p\vec{v}\vec{\omega}q\vec{u}]-[2\vec{\omega}q\vec{v}q\vec{u}]=0$

$\Rightarrow (3p^{2}-pq+2q^{2})[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{\omega}]=0$

$\Rightarrow 3p^{2}-pq+2q^{2}=0$ $($ As $[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{\omega}] \ne 0$ $)$

$\Rightarrow 2p^{2}+p^{2}-pq+\frac{q^{2}}{4}+\frac{7q^{2}}{4}=0$

$\Rightarrow 2p^{2}+(p-\frac{q}{2})^{2}+\frac{7}{4}q^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow p=0,q=0,p=\frac{q}{2}$ $\Rightarrow p=0,q=0$

$\therefore$ Exactly one value of $(p,q)$

questions.question_html: A particle acted on by constant forces $4\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ is displaced from the point $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ to the point $5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+\hat{k}.$ The total work done by the forces is :
questions.explanation_text: The work done by a force on a particle is given by the dot product of the force and the displacement vector of the particle. The displacement vector can be found by subtracting the initial position from the final position: $displacement=finalposition-initialposition=(5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+\hat{k})-(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ The total work done by the two forces is equal to the sum of the work done by each force. The work done by each force can be calculated as the dot product of the force and the displacement: $workdonebyforce𝟏=(4\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \cdot (4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})=4 \cdot 4+1 \cdot 2-3 \cdot -2=16+2+6=24$ $workdonebyforce𝟐=(3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot (4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})=3 \cdot 4+1 \cdot 2-1 \cdot -2=12+2+2=16$ The total work done by the forces is the sum of the work done by each force: $totalworkdone=24+16=40$ Therefore, the total work done by the forces is 40 J (joules) or 40 units.

The work done by a force on a particle is given by the dot product of the force and the displacement vector of the particle. The displacement vector can be found by subtracting the initial position from the final position:

$displacement=finalposition-initialposition=(5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+\hat{k})-(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})=4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$

The total work done by the two forces is equal to the sum of the work done by each force. The work done by each force can be calculated as the dot product of the force and the displacement:

$workdonebyforce𝟏=(4\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}) \cdot (4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})=4 \cdot 4+1 \cdot 2-3 \cdot -2=16+2+6=24$

$workdonebyforce𝟐=(3\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \cdot (4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})=3 \cdot 4+1 \cdot 2-1 \cdot -2=12+2+2=16$

The total work done by the forces is the sum of the work done by each force:

$totalworkdone=24+16=40$

Therefore, the total work done by the forces is 40 J (joules) or 40 units.

questions.question_html: If $\vec{u},\vec{v}$ and $\vec{w}$ are three non-coplanar vectors, then $(\vec{u}+\vec{v}-\vec{w}).(\vec{u}-\vec{v}) \times (\vec{v}-\vec{w})$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: $(\vec{u}+\vec{v}-\vec{w}).(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}-\vec{u} \times \vec{w}-\vec{v} \times \vec{v}+\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$ $=(\vec{u}+\vec{v}-\vec{w}).(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}-\vec{u} \times \vec{w}+\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=\vec{u}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})$ $-\vec{u}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})+\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})+\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})-\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})$ $+\vec{v}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})+\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})$ $=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})-\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})$ $=[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{w})]+[\vec{v}\vec{w}\vec{u})]-[\vec{w}\vec{u}\vec{v}]$ $=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$
questions.explanation_html:
$(\vec{u}+\vec{v}-\vec{w}).(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}-\vec{u} \times \vec{w}-\vec{v} \times \vec{v}+\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$

$=(\vec{u}+\vec{v}-\vec{w}).(\vec{u} \times \vec{v}-\vec{u} \times \vec{w}+\vec{v} \times \vec{w})=\vec{u}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})$

$-\vec{u}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})+\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})+\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})-\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})$

$+\vec{v}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})+\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})$

$=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})-\vec{v}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{w})-\vec{w}.(\vec{u} \times \vec{v})$

$=[\vec{u}\vec{v}\vec{w})]+[\vec{v}\vec{w}\vec{u})]-[\vec{w}\vec{u}\vec{v}]$

$=\vec{u}.(\vec{v} \times \vec{w})$

questions.question_html: Let $\vec{u}=\hat{i}+\hat{j},\vec{v}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ and $\vec{w}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}.$ If $\hat{n}$ is a unit vector such that $\vec{u}.\hat{n}=0$ and $\vec{v}.\hat{n}=0,$ then $|\vec{w}.\hat{n}|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Since, $\hat{n}⟂\vec{u}$ and $\hat{n}⟂\vec{v}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \hat{n} & =\frac{\vec{u} \times \vec{v}}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|} \\ \\ \therefore |\vec{w} \cdot \hat{n}| & =|\frac{\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|}| \\ \\ & =\frac{|\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})|}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})=|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \end{aligned}|=-6 \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow |\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})|=6 \\ \\ \text{and}\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times (\hat{i}-\hat{j})-2\hat{k} \\ \\ \Rightarrow |\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|=2 \\ \\ \therefore |\vec{w} \cdot \hat{n}|=\frac{6}{2}=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Since, $\hat{n}⟂\vec{u}$ and $\hat{n}⟂\vec{v}$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \hat{n} & =\frac{\vec{u} \times \vec{v}}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|} \\ \\ \therefore |\vec{w} \cdot \hat{n}| & =|\frac{\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|}| \\ \\ & =\frac{|\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})|}{|\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Now,}\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})=|\begin{aligned} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \end{aligned}|=-6 \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow |\vec{w} \cdot (\vec{u} \times \vec{v})|=6 \\ \\ \text{and}\vec{u} \times \vec{v}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times (\hat{i}-\hat{j})-2\hat{k} \\ \\ \Rightarrow |\vec{u} \times \vec{v}|=2 \\ \\ \therefore |\vec{w} \cdot \hat{n}|=\frac{6}{2}=3 \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_html:
To solve this problem, let's take it step by step, beginning with calculating each of the vector magnitudes (or norms) and then finding the magnitude of the cross product vector $\vec{c}$ .

Given vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are:

$\vec{a}=3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}$

$\vec{b}=6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$

  1. Magnitude of $\vec{a}$

The magnitude of vector $\vec{a}$ is calculated using the formula:

$|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(-5)^{2}}=\sqrt{9+25}=\sqrt{34}.$

  1. Magnitude of $\vec{b}$

Similarly, the magnitude of vector $\vec{b}$ is calculated as:

$|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{(6)^{2}+(3)^{2}}=\sqrt{36+9}=\sqrt{45}.$

  1. Calculating $\vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$

The cross product of two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ in 3-dimensional space is given by:

$\vec{c}=\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=|\begin{aligned} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -5 & 0 \\ 6 & 3 & 0 \end{aligned}|$

For our provided vectors, the $k$ component of both vectors is $0$ , thus their cross product will be purely in the $k$ direction. The determinant simplifies to:

$\vec{c}=(3 \times 3-(-5) \times 6)\hat{k}=(9+30)\hat{k}=39\hat{k}.$

  1. Magnitude of $\vec{c}$

The magnitude of vector $\vec{c}$ is:

$|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{39^{2}}=39.$

Finally, the ratio of the magnitudes of vectors $\vec{a}$ , $\vec{b}$ , and $\vec{c}$ is thus:

$\sqrt{34}:\sqrt{45}:39.$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option B) $\sqrt{34}:\sqrt{45}:39.$
